board_events.text: For which of these glasses does the ray undergo total internal reflection: $n = 1.30$, $n = 1.40$, or $n = 1.50$?
Total internal reflection at $45^{\circ}$ needs $45^{\circ} \gt C$, that is $\sin 45^{\circ} \gt \sin C = 1/n$.
Only $n = 1.50$ clears the bar, so that is the answer.
The trap: computing $C = \arcsin(1/n)$ three separate times. The comparison collapses all of it into one line.
This is the standard condition for a $45^{\circ}$ totally reflecting prism, so it is worth carrying as a reflex.

segments.text: Now a speed trap, and the lesson is about recognising a condition rather than grinding through three calculations.
The board sets the situation on the left and lists three candidate glasses on the right. Only one card is highlighted; see whether you can pick it before the algebra.
The question. A ray inside glass strikes the glass-air face at forty five degrees. For which glass does it undergo total internal reflection: index one point three, one point four, or one point five?
Set up the condition, not the calculation. Reflection at forty five degrees requires forty five to exceed the critical angle, so the sine of forty five must exceed the sine of C, which is one over n.
The sine of forty five is one over root two, so one over root two must exceed one over n. Inverting gives n greater than root two, about one point four one four.
Now read the options against that bar. One point three fails, one point four fails, one point five clears it. No arcsine was ever needed.
The trap is what it looks like. Students compute the critical angle as the inverse sine of one over n three separate times, then compare. Three calculator operations where one comparison suffices.

Carry this as a reflex; it is the standard condition for a forty five degree totally reflecting prism. Whenever forty five degrees appears at a glass boundary, ask only whether the index beats root two.
अब एक speed trap, और सबक़ ये है कि condition पहचानिए, तीन हिसाब पीसिए मत।
Board बाईं तरफ़ स्थिति बनाता है और दाईं तरफ़ तीन candidate glasses गिनाता है। सिर्फ़ एक card उभरा है, देखिए क्या आप algebra से पहले उसे चुन पाते हैं।
सवाल ये है। Glass के अंदर एक ray glass air face पर पैंतालीस degrees पर टकराती है। किस glass में total internal reflection होगा, index one point three, one point four, या one point five?
हिसाब के बजाय condition बनाइए। पैंतालीस degrees critical angle से बड़ा होना चाहिए, यानी पैंतालीस का sine, sine C से बड़ा हो, और वो है एक बटा n।
पैंतालीस का sine है एक बटा root two, तो एक बटा root two को एक बटा n से बड़ा होना चाहिए। उलटने पर मिलता है n बड़ा root two से, लगभग one point four one four।
अब options को उस पैमाने पर पढ़िए। One point three नाकाम, one point four नाकाम, one point five पार कर जाता है। Arcsine की ज़रूरत ही नहीं पड़ी।
जाल वैसा ही है जैसा दिखता है। Students critical angle को एक बटा n का inverse sine मानकर तीन बार निकालते हैं, फिर तुलना करते हैं। तीन operations वहाँ जहाँ एक तुलना काफ़ी थी।
इसे reflex की तरह रखिए, पैंतालीस degree वाले totally reflecting prism की standard condition यही है। Glass boundary पर पैंतालीस degrees दिखे तो बस पूछिए, index root two को हराता है या नहीं।

board_events.text: A ray is incident at $60^{\circ}$ on a parallel glass slab of refractive index $\sqrt{3}$ and thickness 9 cm. Find the angle of refraction and the lateral shift.
So the angle of refraction is $30^{\circ}$ and the emergent beam is displaced about 5.20 cm sideways.
Note the clean collapse: when $i-r = r$, the expression $\sin(i-r)/\cos r$ becomes $\tan r$. That is a useful flag that the geometry simplified.

segments.text: This combines Snell's law with slab geometry, which is why it sits at main level. Two steps, each short.
The figure carries the numbers. Follow the ray in at sixty degrees, across the slab at thirty, and out parallel to where it started but shifted along the red arrow.
The question. A ray is incident at sixty degrees on a parallel-sided slab of index root three and thickness nine centimetres. Find the angle of refraction and the lateral shift.
Step one, Snell at the first face. The sine of sixty equals root three times the sine of r. The sine of sixty is root three over two, so dividing leaves one half, and r is thirty degrees.
Step two, the lateral shift formula: thickness times the sine of i minus r, over the cosine of r. Here i minus r is thirty degrees.
So we need nine times the sine of thirty over the cosine of thirty. The halves cancel, leaving nine over root three, which is three root three, about five point two centimetres.
State it cleanly. The angle of refraction is thirty degrees, and the emergent beam is displaced about five point two zero centimetres from its no-slab path.
One thing worth noticing. Because i minus r equalled r here, the expression collapsed to the tangent of thirty degrees. Spotting that collapse signals the geometry has simplified.
ये सवाल Snell's law को slab geometry से जोड़ता है, इसीलिए main level पर बैठता है। दो steps, दोनों छोटे।
Figure पर numbers पहले से हैं। Ray साठ degrees पर अंदर जाती है, slab में तीस पर पार करती है, और उसी दिशा में बाहर निकलती है, बस लाल तीर के साथ खिसकी हुई।
सवाल ये है। Index root three और मोटाई नौ centimetres वाली समानांतर slab पर एक ray साठ degrees पर पड़ती है। Angle of refraction और lateral shift निकालिए।
पहला step, पहली face पर Snell. साठ का sine बराबर root three गुणा r का sine. साठ का sine है root three बटा दो, तो भाग देने पर बचता है एक बटा दो, और r बनता है तीस degrees।
दूसरा step, lateral shift वाला formula, यानी मोटाई गुणा sine of i minus r बटा cosine r. यहाँ i minus r है तीस degrees।
तो चाहिए नौ गुणा तीस का sine बटा तीस का cosine. आधे cancel हो जाते हैं और बचता है नौ बटा root three, यानी तीन root three, लगभग पाँच point दो centimetres।
साफ़ लिखिए। Angle of refraction तीस degrees है, और emergent beam अपने बिना slab वाले रास्ते से लगभग पाँच point दो शून्य centimetre खिसक जाती है।
एक बात ध्यान देने लायक़। यहाँ i minus r संयोग से r के बराबर निकला, इसलिए expression सिमटकर तीस degrees का tangent बन गया। ये सिकुड़न दिखे तो geometry सरल हो चुकी है।

board_events.text: Derive and evaluate the acceptance angle: the maximum half-angle of the cone of light, entering from air, that the fibre will guide.
Light enters the flat end face at angle $\theta$ to the axis and refracts to $\alpha$ inside the core. It then strikes the core-cladding wall at $90^{\circ}-\alpha$ to that wall's normal.
For guiding, that wall angle must be at least the critical angle for the core-cladding pair, where $\sin C = n_2/n_1$.
Only rays entering within about a twenty degree half-cone of the axis are trapped. That is exactly why fibre connectors must be precisely aligned.

segments.text: Advanced level, and this one is satisfying, because a messy two-interface chain collapses into one compact expression.
Trace the ray. It enters through the flat end face, bends toward the axis, then strikes the core-cladding wall and is totally reflected onward down the fibre.
The task. A step-index fibre has core index one point five zero and cladding one point four six. Derive and evaluate the acceptance angle, the maximum half-angle of the cone the fibre will guide.

The reasoning spans two interfaces. Light enters at angle theta to the axis and refracts to a smaller alpha inside the core, then meets the core-cladding wall at ninety degrees minus alpha from that wall's normal.
To be guided rather than leak away, that wall angle must be at least the critical angle for the pair, where the sine of C is the cladding index over the core index.
Take the limiting case, the wall angle equal to C. Then alpha is ninety degrees minus C, so the sine of alpha equals the cosine of C, the root of one minus the ratio of the squared indices.
Now apply Snell at the entry face. The sine of theta max equals the core index times the sine of alpha, and on substituting, the core index moves inside the root and the denominators cancel.

What survives is the numerical aperture: the root of the core index squared minus the cladding index squared. The numbers give zero point one one eight four, whose root is about zero point three four four, so the acceptance angle is about twenty point one degrees.
Read the physics out. Only rays entering within roughly a twenty degree half-cone of the axis are guided down the fibre. That is why fibre connectors must be aligned so accurately.
Advanced level, और ये सवाल संतोष देता है, क्योंकि दो interfaces की उलझी कड़ी सिमटकर एक छोटे expression में बदल जाती है।
Ray का पीछा कीजिए। वो सपाट end face से घुसती है, axis की तरफ़ मुड़ती है, फिर core cladding दीवार से टकराकर पूरी परावर्तित होकर fibre में आगे बढ़ती है।
काम ये है। एक step index fibre का core index one point five zero और cladding one point four six है। Acceptance angle derive कीजिए, यानी उस cone का सबसे बड़ा half angle जिसे fibre संभाल लेगा।
तर्क दो interfaces पर फैला है। Light axis से theta कोण पर घुसती है और core में छोटे alpha तक मुड़ जाती है, फिर core cladding दीवार से नब्बे degrees minus alpha पर मिलती है।
Guide होने के लिए वो दीवार वाला कोण उस जोड़ी के critical angle से कम नहीं होना चाहिए, जहाँ sine C बराबर cladding index बटा core index है।
Limiting case लीजिए, दीवार वाला कोण ठीक C. तब alpha बनता है नब्बे degrees minus C, यानी alpha का sine बराबर C का cosine, जो है एक minus squared indices के ratio का root।
अब entry face पर Snell लगाइए। Theta max का sine बराबर core index गुणा alpha का sine, और substitute करने पर core index root के अंदर घुसकर denominators cancel कर देता है।

जो बचता है वही numerical aperture है, core index के square minus cladding index के square का root. Numbers देते हैं zero point one one eight four, जिसका root लगभग zero point three four four है, तो acceptance angle लगभग बीस point एक degrees।
अब physics पढ़िए। सिर्फ़ वही rays आगे जाती हैं जो axis के लगभग बीस degree half cone के अंदर घुसती हैं। इसीलिए fibre connectors इतनी सटीकता से align होते हैं।

board_events.text: Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal. A ray at $30^{\circ}$ to the surface has $i = 60^{\circ}$, and this single slip wrecks otherwise perfect solutions.
Forgetting the direction requirement. Total internal reflection is impossible rarer to denser, so check the medium order before hunting for a critical angle.
Inverting the critical-angle formula. It is $\sin C = 1/n$, never $n = \sin C$. If you ever get $n \lt 1$ for a real material, you have flipped it.
Assuming apparent depth works at any viewing angle. $d' = d/n$ is a near-normal result; steep oblique viewing needs the full Snell geometry.
Reflex one: for the standard $45^{\circ}$ totally reflecting prism, reflection is total if and only if $n \gt \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$.
Reflex two: small $C$ means large $n$. A twenty-four degree critical angle must belong to a high-index material like diamond.
Memory aids: slower means bends toward; denser to rarer and over the critical; small angle, big index.

segments.text: Four pitfalls to close this subtopic, then two reflexes that save real time in the exam hall.
The board holds both halves. On the left, the commonest measuring error. On the right, the direction test and the formula most often written upside down.

First, measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal. A ray at thirty degrees to the surface has an incidence angle of sixty. This slip wrecks otherwise perfect solutions, and it is entirely avoidable.
Second, forgetting the direction requirement. Total internal reflection is impossible rarer to denser, whatever the angle. Check the medium order before hunting for a critical angle.
Third, inverting the critical-angle formula. The sine of C equals one over n, never n equals the sine of C. An index below one for a real material means you flipped it.
Fourth, assuming apparent depth works at any viewing angle. Apparent depth over n is a near-normal result only; steep oblique viewing needs the full Snell geometry.
Now the first reflex. For the standard forty five degree totally reflecting prism, reflection is total if and only if the index exceeds root two. Skip the per-case critical angle entirely.

The second reflex is qualitative but eliminates options on sight. A small critical angle means a large index, so twenty four degrees must belong to a high-index material, which in a physics paper means diamond.

Finally the memory aids. Slower means bends toward: entering a denser, slower medium, the ray bends toward the normal. Denser to rarer, and over the critical, both boxes ticked. And small angle, big index.
इस subtopic को बंद करने के लिए चार pitfalls, फिर दो reflexes जो exam hall में समय बचाएँगे।
Board पर दोनों हिस्से हैं। बाईं तरफ़ सबसे आम नापने वाली ग़लती, दाईं तरफ़ direction test और वो formula जिसे सबसे ज़्यादा उल्टा लिखा जाता है।
पहला, angles को normal के बजाय surface से नापना। Surface से तीस degrees वाली ray का incidence angle साठ degrees होता है। यही चूक बाक़ी सही solution बर्बाद कर देती है, और ये टाली जा सकती है।
दूसरा, direction वाली शर्त भूलना। Rarer से denser जाते हुए total internal reflection मुमकिन नहीं, चाहे angle कितना बड़ा हो। Critical angle ढूँढने से पहले mediums का क्रम जाँचिए।
तीसरा, critical angle का formula उल्टा लिखना। C का sine बराबर है एक बटा n, कभी n बराबर sine C नहीं। असली material के लिए index एक से कम आए तो आपने relation पलट दिया है।
चौथा, ये मानना कि apparent depth हर viewing angle पर चलता है। Real depth बटा n सिर्फ़ near normal नतीजा है, तिरछा देखने पर पूरी Snell geometry चाहिए।
अब पहला reflex. पैंतालीस degree वाले standard totally reflecting prism में reflection पूरा तभी होता है जब index root two से बड़ा हो। हर case का critical angle निकालना छोड़ दीजिए।
दूसरा reflex qualitative है पर देखते ही options काट देता है। छोटा critical angle मतलब बड़ा index, तो चौबीस degrees किसी ऊँचे index वाले material का होगा, और physics के paper में उसका मतलब diamond है।

आख़िर में memory aids. धीमा मतलब normal की तरफ़ मुड़ाव, यानी denser और धीमे medium में घुसते हुए ray normal की तरफ़ मुड़ती है। Denser से rarer, और critical से ऊपर, दोनों खाने भरने चाहिए। और छोटा angle, बड़ा index।

board_events.text: Every refraction so far happened at a flat boundary. But the most useful optical device of all, the lens, is built from curved refracting surfaces.
A curved surface bends each ray by a different amount depending on where it strikes, gathering or spreading them so they seem to come from a new point.
The image position depends on just three things: the two refractive indices on either side, and the radius of curvature $R$.

board_events.text: As $R$ grows without limit the right-hand side vanishes, leaving $n_2/v = n_1/u$, which is exactly the apparent-depth result.
So the curved-surface formula does not replace what you learned. It generalises it. Curvature is what lets a surface focus light instead of merely shifting it.

segments.text: Everything we have refracted so far crossed a flat boundary. But the most useful optical device of all, the lens, is built entirely from curved refracting surfaces.
The picture shows the simplest possible case: one curved boundary, a rarer medium on the left, a denser one on the right, and a single paraxial ray crossing it.
To understand a lens we first have to understand what one curved surface does. Then we simply do it twice. That is the whole plan of this subtopic.
Picture looking at a fish through the rounded glass wall of an aquarium. The fish appears shifted and resized, because light from it refracts as it crosses that curved boundary.
A curved surface bends each ray by a different amount depending on where it strikes, gathering or spreading them so they appear to come from a new point.
The position of that new point depends on three things only: the refractive indices on either side, and the radius of curvature of the surface. They combine into one tidy relation.
Now think about the special case on the right. A flat surface is simply a spherical one whose radius has grown infinite, its centre of curvature pushed away for ever.
Put that in and the right-hand side collapses to zero, leaving the image-side index over v equal to the object-side index over u. That is precisely the apparent-depth result.
So this formula does not replace what you learned; it generalises it. Curvature is exactly what lets a surface focus light rather than merely shift its apparent position.
अब तक हमने जितने refraction देखे, सब flat boundary पर हुए। पर सबसे काम का optical device, यानी lens, पूरी तरह curved refracting surfaces से बना होता है।
Picture सबसे सरल case दिखाती है, एक curved boundary, बाईं तरफ़ rarer medium, दाईं तरफ़ denser, और उसे पार करती एक paraxial ray।
Lens समझने के लिए पहले ये समझना होगा कि एक curved surface क्या करती है। फिर हम वही दो बार कर देंगे। इस subtopic का पूरा plan यही है।
Aquarium की गोल काँच की दीवार से मछली देखिए। मछली खिसकी हुई और आकार बदली दिखती है, क्योंकि उससे आती light उस curved boundary पर refract होती है।
Curved surface हर ray को अलग मात्रा में मोड़ती है, इसलिए rays सिमटकर या फैलकर किसी नए point से आती हुई लगती हैं।
उस नए point की जगह सिर्फ़ तीन चीज़ों पर निर्भर है, दोनों तरफ़ के refractive indices, और surface का radius of curvature. ये तीनों एक सुंदर relation में जुड़ जाते हैं।
अब दाईं तरफ़ वाला special case सोचिए। Flat surface असल में वही spherical surface है जिसका radius अनंत हो गया, centre of curvature हमेशा के लिए दूर धकेल दिया गया।
इसे relation में रखिए तो right hand side शून्य हो जाता है, और बचता है image side index बटा v बराबर object side index बटा u. यही apparent depth वाला नतीजा है।
तो ये formula पुराने को हटाता नहीं, उसे general बनाता है। Curvature ही वो चीज़ है जो surface को सिर्फ़ खिसकाने के बजाय focus करने लायक़ बनाती है।

board_events.text: A thin lens is two refracting surfaces back to back, with glass in between and air, usually, outside.
Light refracts once entering the glass and again leaving it. Apply the single-surface relation at each face and add the two results.
Almost everything cancels, and what is left is the lens-maker's formula.
This is a remarkable statement: the focal length of a lens, its entire optical personality, is fixed by just two things, the material $n$ and the shape $R_1$, $R_2$.
A lens grinder choosing glass and curvatures is literally dialling in a focal length, which is why the formula carries that name.
Because the lens is thin, both refractions are treated as happening at essentially the same plane.

segments.text: Now we build a lens, and the construction is almost disappointingly simple: take what we just derived and use it twice.
The picture shows the assembly. One surface curving one way, a second curving the other, and on the right the two of them fused into a single thin lens.
A thin lens is two refracting surfaces back to back, with glass in between and air, usually, on the outside. There is nothing else to it.
Light refracts once on entering the glass and again on leaving it. So we apply the single-surface relation at each face in turn, and add the two results together.
When we do that, almost everything cancels, including the intermediate image we never actually see. What is left standing is the lens-maker's formula.
Read it slowly, because it is a remarkable statement. A lens's focal length, its entire optical personality, is fixed by just two things: material and shape.
The material enters as the refractive index, and the shape enters as the two radii of curvature. Nothing else about the lens matters, not its diameter, not its mass.
A lens grinder choosing a glass and a pair of curvatures is literally dialling in a focal length. That is exactly why the formula carries the lens-maker's name.
One assumption works quietly throughout. Because the lens is thin, both refractions are treated as happening at the same plane, which is what lets the two equations add so cleanly.
अब हम lens बनाते हैं, और ये बनावट लगभग निराश करने वाली हद तक सरल है, जो अभी निकाला उसे दो बार इस्तेमाल कर लीजिए।
Picture assembly दिखाती है। एक surface एक तरफ़ मुड़ी, दूसरी दूसरी तरफ़, और दाईं तरफ़ दोनों मिलकर एक thin lens बन गईं।
Thin lens दो refracting surfaces हैं, आमने सामने, बीच में glass और बाहर आमतौर पर हवा। इससे ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं।
Light glass में घुसते वक़्त एक बार refract होती है और निकलते वक़्त दोबारा। तो हम single surface वाला relation दोनों faces पर बारी बारी लगाकर दोनों नतीजे जोड़ देते हैं।
ऐसा करते ही लगभग सब कुछ cancel हो जाता है, वो intermediate image भी जो हम कभी देखते ही नहीं। जो खड़ा रह जाता है वही lens maker का formula है।
इसे धीरे पढ़िए, ये बयान कमाल का है। Lens की focal length, यानी उसका पूरा optical व्यक्तित्व, सिर्फ़ दो चीज़ों से तय होता है, material और shape।
Material refractive index बनकर आता है और shape दोनों radii of curvature बनकर। Lens के बारे में और कुछ मायने नहीं रखता, न उसका diameter, न वज़न।
Glass और दो curvatures चुनता हुआ lens grinder असल में focal length dial कर रहा होता है। इसीलिए इस formula पर lens maker का नाम चढ़ा है।
एक assumption चुपचाप काम कर रहा है। Lens पतला है, इसलिए दोनों refractions एक ही plane पर माने जाते हैं, और इसी से दोनों equations सफ़ाई से जुड़ते हैं।

board_events.text: The $(n-1)$ factor is really $\left(\dfrac{n_{\text{lens}}}{n_{\text{medium}}}-1\right)$. In air the denominator is one, so it hides.
Dip a glass lens in water and that factor shrinks dramatically, so the lens becomes much weaker and its focal length grows.
Push it to the extreme. A lens made of ice in water, or glass in a liquid of the same index, stops working as a lens at all.
Second consequence: the same lens can converge or diverge depending on the medium.
An air bubble in water is shaped like a convex lens but actually diverges light, because the lens is now rarer than its surroundings.
So convex does not mean converging. Thicker at the centre and denser than its surroundings means converging.

segments.text: Two consequences of that formula are worth feeling in your bones before we touch any algebra, because both of them are favourite examination traps.
The three panels show the whole story: the same glass lens in air, the same lens in water, and finally an air bubble sitting in water.
Here is the first consequence. The bracket we wrote as n minus one is really the lens index divided by the medium index, minus one. In air the denominator is one, so it hides.
Write it out in full and the medium is suddenly visible. That general form is the one that governs every lens-dipped-in-liquid problem you will ever meet.
Dip a glass lens in water and that factor shrinks dramatically, because glass and water are far closer in index than glass and air. The lens becomes much weaker and its focal length grows.
Push it to the extreme and something striking happens. A glass lens in a liquid of exactly the same index stops working as a lens altogether.
The second consequence is stranger still. The same lens can converge or diverge, depending entirely on what surrounds it.
An air bubble in water is shaped exactly like a convex lens, yet it diverges light, because the lens is now rarer than its surroundings and the index contrast has reversed sign.
So carry the corrected rule. Convex does not mean converging. Thicker at the centre and denser than its surroundings means converging. Change either half and the behaviour flips.
उस formula के दो नतीजे algebra छूने से पहले ही अच्छी तरह महसूस कर लीजिए, क्योंकि दोनों exam के पसंदीदा जाल हैं।
तीनों panels पूरी कहानी दिखाते हैं, वही glass lens हवा में, वही lens पानी में, और आख़िर में पानी के अंदर बैठा एक air bubble।
पहला नतीजा ये है। जिस bracket को हमने n minus one लिखा, वो असल में lens का index बटा medium का index, minus one है। हवा में denominator एक होता है, इसलिए वो छिप जाता है।
पूरा लिख दीजिए तो medium अचानक दिखने लगता है। यही general रूप हर lens dipped in liquid वाले सवाल को चलाता है।
Glass lens को पानी में डुबोइए तो वो factor बहुत घट जाता है, क्योंकि glass और पानी के indices, glass और हवा के मुक़ाबले बहुत पास हैं। Lens कमज़ोर हो जाता है और focal length बढ़ जाती है।
अब इसे हद तक ले जाइए और कुछ चौंकाने वाला होता है। ठीक उसी index वाले liquid में रखा glass lens, lens की तरह काम करना ही बंद कर देता है।
दूसरा नतीजा और भी अजीब है। वही lens converge भी कर सकता है और diverge भी, पूरी तरह इस पर कि उसके चारों तरफ़ क्या है।
पानी में air bubble बिल्कुल convex lens जैसा दिखता है, फिर भी light फैलाता है, क्योंकि अब lens आसपास से rarer है और index contrast का sign उलट गया है।
तो सुधरा हुआ नियम याद रखिए। Convex का मतलब converging नहीं होता। बीच में मोटा और आसपास से denser होना converging बनाता है। इनमें से एक भी बदलिए तो बर्ताव पलट जाता है।

board_events.text: Always take light as travelling from left to right. Every sign in this subtopic follows from that one choice.
For each surface, ask a single question: on which side does its centre of curvature lie?
Centre of curvature on the outgoing side means $R$ is positive. On the incoming side means $R$ is negative.
So for a biconvex lens $R_1 \gt 0$ and $R_2 \lt 0$. For a biconcave lens $R_1 \lt 0$ and $R_2 \gt 0$.
A flat surface has infinite radius and therefore contributes nothing to the bracket.
The sign convention matters more here than anywhere else in the chapter, because two indices and two radii all carry signs at once.
Get them right and the lens-maker's formula automatically delivers a positive $f$ for converging lenses and a negative one for diverging lenses.

segments.text: Before any numerical, the sign convention. It matters more in this subtopic than anywhere else in the chapter, because two indices and two radii all carry signs at once.
The board shows three lens shapes with their radii labelled, and on the right the single question that settles every one of them.
Rule one, and it is a choice we simply make and never abandon. Always take the light as travelling from left to right. Every sign that follows comes out of that one decision.
Rule two. For each surface in turn, ask one question and one question only: on which side of that surface does its own centre of curvature lie?
If the centre of curvature sits on the outgoing side, the radius is positive. If on the incoming side, it is negative. That is the whole convention.

Run it on a biconvex lens. The first face bulges toward the light, so its centre is off to the right and its radius is positive. The second face has its centre back on the left, so its radius is negative.
A flat face is the easy one. Its radius is infinite, so one over that radius is zero, and it contributes nothing at all to the bracket. Plano lenses lose a whole term.
Notice how easy the mistake is. Both faces of a biconvex lens look convex, so it feels natural to give both radii the same sign, and that single slip collapses the formula.

Get the signs right and something satisfying happens. The lens-maker's formula then delivers a positive focal length for converging lenses and a negative one for diverging lenses, entirely on its own.
किसी भी numerical से पहले sign convention. ये इस subtopic में chapter के बाक़ी हिस्सों से भी ज़्यादा मायने रखता है, क्योंकि यहाँ दो indices और दो radii, चारों एक साथ signs लेकर चलते हैं।
Board पर तीन lens shapes हैं, radii के साथ, और दाईं तरफ़ वो एक सवाल जो इन सबको तय कर देता है।
पहला rule, और ये सिर्फ़ एक चुनाव है जिसे हम कभी नहीं छोड़ते। Light हमेशा बाएँ से दाएँ चल रही मानिए। आगे के सारे signs इसी एक फ़ैसले से निकलते हैं।
दूसरा rule. हर surface के लिए बारी बारी सिर्फ़ एक सवाल पूछिए, उस surface का अपना centre of curvature किस तरफ़ है?
Centre of curvature outgoing तरफ़ हो तो radius positive, incoming तरफ़ हो तो negative. बस यही पूरा convention है।
इसे biconvex lens पर चलाइए। पहली face light की तरफ़ उभरी है, तो centre दाईं ओर और radius positive. दूसरी face का centre बाईं ओर, तो radius negative.
Flat face सबसे आसान है। उसका radius अनंत है, तो एक बटा radius शून्य, और वो bracket में कुछ भी नहीं जोड़ता। Plano lenses में एक पूरा term ग़ायब हो जाता है।
ध्यान दीजिए ग़लती कितनी आसान है। Biconvex lens की दोनों faces convex दिखती हैं, इसलिए दोनों radii को एक ही sign देना स्वाभाविक लगता है, और यही एक चूक formula को ढहा देती है।
Signs सही कर लीजिए तो एक संतोष देने वाली बात होती है। फिर lens maker का formula ख़ुद ही converging lenses को positive focal length और diverging को negative दे देता है।

board_events.text: A convex surface of radius $R$ separates a rarer medium $n_1$ on the left from a denser $n_2$ on the right, with the centre of curvature $C$ on the right.
A paraxial ray from an axial object $O$ strikes the surface at $M$, a small height $h$ above the axis, and refracts to form the image $I$.
Let $\alpha = \angle MOP$, $\beta = \angle MIP$ and $\theta = \angle MCP$, with $i$ and $r$ the angles of incidence and refraction.
For paraxial rays Snell's law linearises to $n_1 i = n_2 r$, giving $n_1\alpha + n_2\beta = (n_2-n_1)\theta$.

segments.text: This derivation is a classic board question worth two or three marks, and it rests on nothing more than the exterior-angle property of a triangle.
The figure carries the argument. One paraxial ray, the point M where it lands, the radius acting as the normal, and three small angles that turn out to be everything.
Set it up. A convex surface of radius R separates a rarer medium on the left from a denser one on the right, with the centre of curvature sitting on the right.
A paraxial ray from an axial point object strikes the surface at M, a small height above the axis, and refracts to form the image further along the axis on the right.
Name the three angles. Alpha is made by the incident ray at the object, beta by the refracted ray at the image, and theta by the radius at the centre of curvature.

Now the exterior-angle property, twice. In the triangle joining object, M and centre it gives the incidence angle as alpha plus theta. In the triangle joining M, image and centre, theta equals the refraction angle plus beta.
For paraxial rays Snell's law linearises, because the sine of a small angle is the angle itself. So the first index times the incidence angle equals the second index times the refraction angle.
Substitute the two triangle results and collect terms. Then use the small-angle approximations: each angle is the height h divided by the relevant distance, with u carrying its negative sign.

Cancel the common height h and the single-surface relation drops straight out. Although derived for a convex surface and a real image, sign consistency makes it universal for any spherical refracting surface.
ये derivation दो तीन marks का classic board सवाल है, और ये triangle की exterior angle property से ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं माँगता।
Figure में पूरा तर्क है। एक paraxial ray, वो point M जहाँ वो गिरती है, normal का काम करती radius, और तीन छोटे angles जो असल में सब कुछ हैं।
Setup बनाइए। Radius R वाली convex surface बाईं तरफ़ के rarer medium को दाईं तरफ़ के denser से अलग करती है, और centre of curvature दाईं ओर बैठा है।
Axis पर रखे point object से एक paraxial ray surface पर M पर टकराती है, axis से थोड़ी ऊँचाई पर, और refract होकर दाईं ओर axis पर image बनाती है।
तीनों angles के नाम रखिए। Alpha incident ray object पर बनाती है, beta refracted ray image पर, और theta radius centre of curvature पर।
अब exterior angle property, दो बार। Object, M और centre वाले triangle में incidence angle बनता है alpha plus theta. M, image और centre वाले triangle में theta बराबर refraction angle plus beta।
Paraxial rays में Snell's law सीधा हो जाता है, क्योंकि छोटे कोण का sine वही कोण होता है। तो पहला index गुणा incidence angle बराबर दूसरा index गुणा refraction angle।
दोनों triangle नतीजे रखकर terms इकट्ठे कीजिए। फिर small angle approximations लगाइए, हर कोण ऊँचाई h बटा उससे जुड़ी दूरी, और u अपना negative sign साथ लाता है।

साझा ऊँचाई h cancel कीजिए और single surface relation सीधे निकल आता है। निकाला convex surface और real image के लिए, पर sign consistency इसे हर spherical refracting surface के लिए universal बना देती है।

<text x="34" y="360" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#b3402f" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Add them and the n / v₁ terms cancel, leaving the lens-maker’s formula.</text>

board_events.text: A thin lens of material index $n$ in air has two surfaces of radii $R_1$ and $R_2$. Treat it as two single-surface refractions in series.
Because the lens is thin, both refractions occur at essentially the same plane.
The intermediate image $v_1$ acts as the object for the second surface. Add the two equations and the $n/v_1$ terms cancel.

segments.text: Now the derivation the boards ask for most often in this subtopic. It is short, and every step is one we have already done once.
Follow the figure. The blue ray enters, the dashed red line shows where the first surface alone would have sent it, and the green line where the second surface actually puts it.
Take a thin lens of material index n sitting in air, with two surfaces of radii R one and R two. Treat it as two single-surface refractions happening one after the other.
Because the lens is thin, both refractions occur at essentially the same plane. That assumption is what lets us reuse the same object and image distances for both equations.
At the first surface, light goes from air into glass. The object sits at u, and the surface would form an intermediate image at v one. Write the single-surface relation for that crossing.
At the second surface, light goes from glass back into air. The key move: that intermediate image acts as the object for the second surface, whether or not it ever forms.
Now add the two equations. The terms carrying v one appear with opposite signs and cancel completely, which is why the intermediate image never shows up in the final answer.
What survives on the left is one over v minus one over u, and on the right the bracket with the two radii. Compare that with the thin-lens definition of focal length.
That comparison gives the lens-maker's formula. And repeating the whole derivation with the lens in a medium replaces the bracket n minus one by n over the medium index, minus one.
अब वो derivation जो इस subtopic में boards सबसे ज़्यादा पूछते हैं। ये छोटी है, और हर step वो है जो हम एक बार कर चुके हैं।
Figure देखिए। नीली ray अंदर जाती है, dashed लाल line दिखाती है पहली surface अकेली उसे कहाँ भेजती, और हरी line बताती है दूसरी ने कहाँ रखा।
हवा में रखा material index n वाला thin lens लीजिए, जिसकी दो surfaces के radii हैं R one और R two. इसे एक के बाद एक होते दो single surface refractions मानिए।
Lens पतला है, इसलिए दोनों refractions लगभग एक ही plane पर होते हैं। यही assumption दोनों equations में एक ही object और image distances इस्तेमाल करने देता है।
पहली surface पर light हवा से glass में जाती है। Object u पर है, और ये surface v one पर एक intermediate image बनाती। उस crossing के लिए single surface relation लिखिए।
दूसरी surface पर light glass से वापस हवा में जाती है। असली चाल यही है, वो intermediate image दूसरी surface का object बन जाता है, चाहे कभी बने ही नहीं।
अब दोनों equations जोड़ दीजिए। v one वाले terms उल्टे signs के साथ आते हैं और पूरी तरह cancel हो जाते हैं, इसीलिए intermediate image आख़िरी जवाब में कहीं नहीं दिखता।
बाईं तरफ़ बचता है one over v minus one over u, और दाईं तरफ़ दोनों radii वाला bracket. इसकी तुलना thin lens की focal length वाली परिभाषा से कीजिए।
इसी तुलना से lens maker का formula निकलता है। और पूरी derivation lens को medium में रखकर दोहराइए तो bracket n minus one की जगह n बटा medium index, minus one आ जाता है।

board_events.text: Tracing the ray through the pole and applying the paraxial Snell relation to the object and image heights gives the magnification.
The extra index ratio, absent in the mirror case, appears because object and image sit in different media.
So the angular sizes scale with the refractive indices as well as with the distances.
Both the single-surface relation and the lens-maker's formula are paraxial: small angles, narrow beams close to the axis.
They also assume a thin lens, one whose thickness is negligible compared with the object and image distances and with the radii.
For thick lenses or wide apertures, aberrations creep in and these clean formulas only approximate reality.

segments.text: One short result completes the toolkit, and then the fine print that tells you when all of this stops being true.
Look at the figure. The object stands in the first medium and the image forms in the second, and that asymmetry is what makes this magnification different from the mirror one.
Trace a ray through the pole of the surface and apply the paraxial Snell relation to the object and image heights. The geometry is the same similar-triangle argument we used for mirrors.
What comes out is the ratio of image height to object height, equal to the first index times v, divided by the second index times u.
Compare that with the mirror, where magnification was simply minus v over u with no indices at all. The extra ratio here is not decoration; it is a real physical difference.
It appears because the object and the image sit in different media. Angular sizes therefore scale with the refractive indices as well as with the distances, and both effects must be carried.
Now the fine print, which examiners do test. Both the single-surface relation and the lens-maker's formula are paraxial results: small angles, narrow beams travelling close to the axis.
They also assume a genuinely thin lens, one whose thickness is negligible compared with the object and image distances, and compared with the radii of curvature themselves.
Push beyond either limit and aberrations creep in. For thick lenses or wide apertures these clean formulas only approximate reality.
एक छोटा नतीजा toolkit पूरा कर देता है, और फिर वो fine print जो बताता है कि ये सब कब सच नहीं रहता।
Figure देखिए। Object पहले medium में है और image दूसरे में, और यही असमानता इस magnification को mirror वाले से अलग बनाती है।
Surface के pole से गुज़रती एक ray लीजिए और object तथा image की heights पर paraxial Snell relation लगाइए। Geometry वही similar triangle वाला तर्क है जो mirrors में इस्तेमाल हुआ।
जो निकलता है वो है image height बटा object height, बराबर पहला index गुणा v, बटा दूसरा index गुणा u.
इसकी तुलना mirror से कीजिए, जहाँ magnification सिर्फ़ minus v बटा u था, कोई index नहीं। यहाँ का अतिरिक्त ratio सजावट नहीं, असली physical फ़र्क़ है।
ये इसलिए आता है क्योंकि object और image अलग अलग media में बैठे हैं। इसलिए angular sizes distances के साथ साथ refractive indices से भी scale होती हैं, और दोनों असर साथ चलते हैं।
अब fine print, जिसे examiners सचमुच जाँचते हैं। Single surface relation और lens maker formula दोनों paraxial नतीजे हैं, छोटे angles और axis के पास चलती पतली beams।
ये सचमुच thin lens भी मानते हैं, यानी ऐसा lens जिसकी मोटाई object तथा image distances के मुक़ाबले, और ख़ुद radii of curvature के मुक़ाबले, नगण्य हो।
कोई भी हद पार कीजिए तो aberrations घुस आते हैं। मोटे lenses या चौड़े apertures में ये formulas सिर्फ़ approximation रह जाते हैं।

board_events.text: Everything this subtopic runs on
Light travels from medium $n_1$ into $n_2$. All of $u$, $v$ and $R$ are measured from the pole of the surface under the New Cartesian convention.

board_events.text: $R_1$ is the radius of the first surface the light meets, $R_2$ of the second. Note the minus sign in the thin-lens formula: refraction subtracts, reflection adds.

segments.text: This is the working set for the subtopic. Four relations, and each of them appears directly in a standard question.
First, refraction at a single spherical surface. Image-side index over image distance, minus object-side index over object distance, equals the index jump divided by the radius.
Pin the symbols down, because swapping them is the commonest error here. Light goes from the first medium into the second, and all three distances are measured from the pole.
Second, the magnification at that single surface. It carries the index ratio as well as the distance ratio, which the mirror version never did.
Third, the lens-maker's formula in air. The focal length is set by the material through the bracket, and by the shape through the two radii. Nothing else about the lens enters.
Fourth, the general form for a lens sitting in a medium. The bracket becomes the lens index divided by the medium index, minus one. Every lens-in-liquid problem needs this version.
The diagram gives you a check that needs no formula at all. Thicker at the centre and denser than its surroundings means converging; thinner at the centre means diverging.
And finally the thin-lens formula itself, which is a direct consequence of the lens-maker relation and which we will use throughout the next subtopic.
Two definitions to fix. R one is the radius of the first surface the light meets, R two of the second. And note that minus sign: refraction subtracts, reflection adds.
ये इस subtopic का working set है। चार relations, और हर एक किसी न किसी standard सवाल में सीधे आता है।
पहला, single spherical surface पर refraction. Image side index बटा image distance, minus object side index बटा object distance, बराबर index का अंतर बटा radius।
Symbols पक्के कीजिए, इन्हें बदल देना यहाँ की सबसे आम ग़लती है। Light पहले medium से दूसरे में जाती है, और तीनों distances pole से नापे जाते हैं।
दूसरा, उसी single surface का magnification. ये distance ratio के साथ index ratio भी लेकर चलता है, जो mirror वाले रूप में कभी नहीं था।
तीसरा, हवा में lens maker का formula. Focal length material से bracket के ज़रिए तय होती है, और shape से दोनों radii के ज़रिए। Lens की और कोई बात इसमें नहीं आती।
चौथा, medium में रखे lens के लिए general रूप। Bracket बन जाता है lens index बटा medium index, minus one. हर lens in liquid वाला सवाल यही रूप माँगता है।
Diagram एक ऐसी जाँच देता है जिसमें formula लगता ही नहीं। बीच में मोटा और आसपास से denser मतलब converging, बीच में पतला मतलब diverging।
और आख़िर में thin lens formula ख़ुद, जो lens maker relation का सीधा नतीजा है और जिसे हम अगले subtopic में लगातार इस्तेमाल करेंगे।
दो परिभाषाएँ तय कीजिए। R one पहली surface का radius है, R two दूसरी का। और उस minus sign पर ध्यान दीजिए, refraction घटाता है, reflection जोड़ता है।

sections.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and the Lens-Maker's Formula
sections.title: Radius signs, shape checks, units and dimensions

board_events.text: The bookkeeping that keeps the toolkit honest
Sign convention for radii, with light travelling left to right: $R$ is positive if the centre of curvature lies on the outgoing side, negative if on the incoming side.
Hence for a biconvex lens $R_1 \gt 0$ and $R_2 \lt 0$; for a biconcave lens $R_1 \lt 0$ and $R_2 \gt 0$.
That ratio form is the fastest route for any lens-dipped-in-liquid question, because the shape factor cancels and the radii are never needed.
Units: $n$ is dimensionless. The lengths $u$, $v$, $f$ and $R$ are metres, $[M^0L^1T^0]$. Magnification is a pure ratio.
A useful shape check: a lens converges, with real positive $f$, when it is thicker at the centre and denser than its surroundings. Otherwise it diverges.

segments.text: The second half of the toolkit is bookkeeping, but it is the bookkeeping that decides whether the first half gives you the right answer.
The radius sign convention, stated once properly. With light travelling left to right, a radius is positive if its centre of curvature lies on the outgoing side, negative if on the incoming side.
Apply it and the standard shapes fall out. A biconvex lens has its first radius positive and its second negative. A biconcave lens has exactly the reverse.
A flat face is the easy case. Its radius is infinite, so one over that radius is zero, and the whole term disappears from the bracket.
Here is a shortcut worth memorising for symmetric lenses, the equiconvex and equiconcave ones. The focal length is simply the radius divided by twice the quantity n minus one.
And here is the shortcut for the other standard question. Take the ratio of the two lens-maker expressions, in medium and in air, and the shape factor cancels completely.
That ratio form is the fastest route for any lens-dipped-in-liquid problem, because you never need the radii at all. We will use it directly in a worked example shortly.
Now the units, which boards ask for. The refractive index is dimensionless. The four lengths are metres, M to the zero, L to the one, T to the zero. Magnification is a pure ratio.
And keep the shape check ready as a final sanity test. A lens converges, with a real positive focal length, when it is thicker at the centre and denser than its surroundings. Otherwise it diverges.
Toolkit का दूसरा आधा हिस्सा हिसाब किताब है, पर यही हिसाब तय करता है कि पहला आधा हिस्सा सही जवाब देगा या नहीं।
Radius का sign convention, एक बार ठीक से। Light बाएँ से दाएँ मानकर, radius positive अगर centre of curvature outgoing तरफ़ हो, negative अगर incoming तरफ़।
इसे लगाइए तो standard shapes ख़ुद निकल आती हैं। Biconvex lens का पहला radius positive और दूसरा negative. Biconcave में बिल्कुल उल्टा।
Flat face आसान case है। उसका radius अनंत है, तो एक बटा radius शून्य, और पूरा term bracket से ग़ायब हो जाता है।
Symmetric lenses, यानी equiconvex और equiconcave, के लिए एक shortcut याद रखने लायक़ है। Focal length बस radius बटा दुगुना n minus one होती है।
और दूसरे standard सवाल के लिए ये shortcut है। Medium और हवा वाले दोनों lens maker expressions का ratio लीजिए, shape factor पूरी तरह cancel हो जाता है।
यही ratio रूप हर lens in liquid वाले सवाल का सबसे तेज़ रास्ता है, क्योंकि radii की ज़रूरत ही नहीं पड़ती। हम इसे थोड़ी देर में एक worked example में सीधे इस्तेमाल करेंगे।
अब units. Refractive index dimensionless है। चारों lengths metres हैं, M to the zero, L to the one, T to the zero. Magnification pure ratio है।
और shape check आख़िरी sanity test की तरह तैयार रखिए। Lens converge करता है, यानी positive focal length देता है, जब वो बीच में मोटा और आसपास से denser हो। वरना वो diverge करता है।

board_events.text: One end of a long glass rod is polished into a convex surface of radius 10 cm. A small object sits in air on the axis, 50 cm from that end.
Given: $n_1 = 1$, $n_2 = 1.5$, and $R = +10$ cm because the centre of curvature lies inside the rod, on the outgoing side. The object is real, so $u = -50$ cm.
A real image forms 50 cm inside the rod. The positive $v$ confirms it lies on the outgoing side, in the glass.
Note there is no lens here at all, and no focal length. A single refracting surface is enough to form an image.

segments.text: Start at board level, where the whole difficulty is in assigning the signs correctly before any arithmetic begins.
The figure shows the situation. Air on the left, the polished convex end of a long glass rod, and the image forming inside the glass on the right.
The question. One end of a long glass rod of index one point five is polished into a convex surface of radius ten centimetres, with a small object in air on the axis fifty centimetres away.
Write the signed data first. The first index is one for air, the second one point five for glass. The radius is plus ten centimetres, its centre of curvature lying inside the rod.
The object is real and sits in front, so its distance is minus fifty centimetres. Now substitute into the single-surface relation, and notice the double negative on the object term becoming a plus.
The right-hand side is the index jump, nought point five, divided by the radius, ten, which is nought point nought five.
Rearranging, one point five over v equals nought point nought five minus nought point nought two, that is nought point nought three.

So v is one point five divided by nought point nought three, which is plus fifty centimetres. A real image forms fifty centimetres inside the rod, and the positive sign confirms it lies on the outgoing side.
One thing worth noticing before we move on. There is no lens here at all, and no focal length anywhere in the working. A single refracting surface is quite enough to form an image.
Board level से शुरू करते हैं, जहाँ पूरी कठिनाई arithmetic से पहले signs सही तय करने में है।
Figure स्थिति दिखाती है। बाईं तरफ़ हवा, लंबे glass rod का polished convex सिरा, और दाईं तरफ़ glass के अंदर बनती image।
सवाल ये है। One point five index वाले glass rod का एक सिरा दस centimetre radius की convex surface में घिसा है, और एक छोटा object हवा में axis पर पचास centimetre दूर है।
पहले signed data लिखिए। पहला index हवा के लिए एक, दूसरा glass के लिए one point five. Radius plus दस centimetres, centre of curvature rod के अंदर।
Object real है और सामने है, तो उसकी दूरी minus पचास centimetres. अब single surface relation में रखिए, और ध्यान दीजिए कि object term का double negative plus बन जाता है।
Right hand side है index का अंतर, नौ के बाद वाला आधा यानी point five, बटा radius दस, जो होता है point zero five।
Rearrange करने पर one point five बटा v बराबर point zero five minus point zero two, यानी point zero three।
तो v है one point five बटा point zero three, यानी plus पचास centimetres. Real image rod के अंदर पचास centimetre पर बनती है, और positive sign बताता है कि वो outgoing तरफ़ है।
आगे बढ़ने से पहले एक बात ध्यान देने लायक़। यहाँ कोई lens है ही नहीं, और पूरी working में कहीं focal length नहीं आई। एक अकेली refracting surface image बनाने के लिए काफ़ी है।

board_events.text: A biconvex lens has both faces of radius 20 cm and is made of glass with $n = 1.5$. Find its focal length.
The trap: forgetting that $R_2$ is negative turns the sum into a difference and gives the wrong, often infinite, answer.
The lens is converging, since $f$ comes out positive.
For any symmetric lens that one-line form skips the sign bookkeeping entirely.

segments.text: This one is built around a single sign, and the sign is the entire question. Everything else is arithmetic you can do in your head.
The picture marks both centres of curvature. The first face has its centre off to the right, the second face has its centre back to the left, and that is what decides the two signs.
The question. A biconvex lens has both faces of radius twenty centimetres and is made of glass with index one point five. Find its focal length.
Here is the trap. Both faces look convex, so it feels natural to write both radii as plus twenty. That turns the sum into a difference and the bracket into zero.
Do it properly. The first radius is plus twenty and the second is minus twenty, so one over the first minus one over the second becomes one twentieth plus one twentieth, which is one tenth.
Then one over f is the bracket, nought point five, times one tenth, which is nought point nought five. So the focal length is twenty centimetres.
The focal length came out positive, which tells you at once the lens is converging. That agrees with the shape: thicker at the centre, denser than the air around it.
Now the shortcut worth carrying. For any symmetric lens the focal length is simply the radius divided by twice the quantity n minus one.
Put the numbers in and it is twenty divided by two times nought point five, which is twenty centimetres, in a single line. For symmetric lenses that form skips the sign bookkeeping entirely.
ये सवाल एक ही sign के इर्द गिर्द बना है, और वही sign पूरा सवाल है। बाक़ी सब मन में हो जाने वाला arithmetic है।
Picture दोनों centres of curvature दिखाती है। पहली face का centre दाईं ओर है, दूसरी face का centre वापस बाईं ओर, और यही दोनों signs तय करता है।
सवाल ये है। एक biconvex lens की दोनों faces का radius बीस centimetre है और वो one point five index वाले glass का बना है। उसकी focal length निकालिए।
यही जाल है। दोनों faces convex दिखती हैं, तो दोनों radii plus बीस लिखना स्वाभाविक लगता है। इससे जोड़ घटाव बन जाता है और bracket शून्य।
सही तरीक़े से कीजिए। पहला radius plus बीस और दूसरा minus बीस, तो एक बटा पहला minus एक बटा दूसरा बनता है एक बटा बीस plus एक बटा बीस, यानी एक बटा दस।
फिर one over f बराबर bracket यानी point five, गुणा एक बटा दस, जो है point zero five. तो focal length बीस centimetres।
Focal length positive आई, जो तुरंत बताती है कि lens converging है। ये shape से भी मेल खाता है, बीच में मोटा और आसपास की हवा से denser।
अब वो shortcut जो साथ रखने लायक़ है। किसी भी symmetric lens की focal length बस radius बटा दुगुना n minus one होती है।
Numbers रखिए तो बीस बटा दो गुणा point five, यानी बीस centimetres, एक ही line में। Symmetric lenses के लिए ये रूप sign वाला पूरा हिसाब बचा देता है।

board_events.text: The lens of the previous example, of focal length 20 cm in air, is now fully immersed in water. Find its new focal length.
Take the ratio of the two lens-maker expressions. The shape factor is identical in both, so it cancels and the radii are never needed.
In water the lens is four times weaker. Physically, the glass-to-water index contrast is far smaller than glass-to-air, so each surface bends light much less.
Notice what the ratio method bought you: no radii, no bracket expansion, and no chance of a radius sign error.

segments.text: Now the main-level version, and it is really a question about method rather than about lenses. Choose the wrong route and it is long; choose the right one and it is three lines.
The two panels show the same lens twice. In air it brings the rays to a focus quickly; in water the focus has slid far out to the right.
The question. The lens of the previous example, focal length twenty centimetres in air and made of glass of index one point five, is now fully immersed in water of index one point three three.
The slow route is to go back to the radii, rebuild the bracket with the new medium, and grind through. The fast route is to take the ratio of the two lens-maker expressions.
That works because the shape factor, the part with the two radii, is identical in both expressions. Divide one by the other and it cancels completely.
So the ratio of focal lengths is the air bracket over the water bracket. The air bracket is nought point five. The water bracket is one point five over one point three three, minus one.
One point five divided by one point three three is one point one two five, so the water bracket is nought point one two five. The ratio is therefore four.
The new focal length is therefore four times twenty, that is eighty centimetres. In water the lens is four times weaker than it was in air.
Read the physics behind it. The glass-to-water contrast is far smaller than glass-to-air, so each surface bends the light much less. And the ratio method needed no radii at all.
अब main level वाला रूप, और ये असल में method का सवाल है, lens का नहीं। ग़लत रास्ता लीजिए तो लंबा, सही लीजिए तो तीन lines।
दोनों panels वही lens दो बार दिखाते हैं। हवा में वो rays को जल्दी focus कर देता है, पानी में focus दाईं ओर बहुत दूर खिसक जाता है।
सवाल ये है। पिछले example वाला lens, हवा में बीस centimetre focal length और one point five index वाले glass का, अब one point three three index वाले पानी में पूरी तरह डुबो दिया गया है।
धीमा रास्ता है radii पर लौटना, नए medium के साथ bracket दोबारा बनाना, और पीसते रहना। तेज़ रास्ता है दोनों lens maker expressions का ratio ले लेना।
ये इसलिए चलता है क्योंकि shape factor, यानी दोनों radii वाला हिस्सा, दोनों expressions में एक जैसा है। एक को दूसरे से भाग दीजिए तो वो पूरी तरह cancel हो जाता है।
तो focal lengths का ratio बनता है हवा वाला bracket बटा पानी वाला bracket. हवा वाला bracket है point five. पानी वाला है one point five बटा one point three three, minus one.
One point five को one point three three से भाग देने पर one point one two five आता है, तो पानी वाला bracket है point one two five, और ratio हुआ चार।
इसलिए नई focal length है चार गुना बीस, यानी अस्सी centimetres. पानी में lens हवा के मुक़ाबले चार गुना कमज़ोर है।
पीछे की physics पढ़िए। Glass से पानी का contrast, glass से हवा के मुक़ाबले बहुत कम है, इसलिए हर surface light को कम मोड़ती है। और ratio method में radii चाहिए ही नहीं।

<text x="180" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#2b6ca3" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">parallel beam along a diameter</text>
<rect x="20" y="316" width="350" height="45" rx="6" fill="#e6ebee"/>
<text x="34" y="334" font-size="12.5" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Surface one sends it toward 3R. Surface two is only 2R away, so that becomes a virtual object at u₂ = +R.</text>
<text x="34" y="350" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#b3402f" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Surface two then gives 1/v = 0.5/R + 1.5/R = 2/R, so v = R/2 beyond the far surface.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: A parallel beam travels along a diameter. This is two single-surface refractions in series, and the second one has a surprise in it.
That would-be image lies $3R$ to the right of surface one. But surface two is only $2R$ away, the diameter, so the image falls $R$ beyond it.
It therefore serves as a virtual object for surface two, at $u_2 = +R$. This is the step the whole problem is built around.
For surface two the radius is $-R$, because its centre of curvature is now on the incoming side.

segments.text: Advanced level, and the elegance here is that the whole problem turns on one idea: an image that never actually forms can still act as an object.
Trace the figure. The beam enters on the left, bends toward the axis, and the faint dashed line shows where the first surface alone would have sent it, well outside the sphere.
The setup. A solid glass sphere of radius R and index one point five sits in air, and a parallel beam travels along a diameter. Treat it as two single-surface refractions in series.
Surface one first. The object is at infinity, so the object term vanishes and one point five over v one equals nought point five over R. That gives v one equal to three R.
So the first surface is trying to form its image three R to the right of the entry point. But the far surface is only two R away, that distance being the diameter.
The light therefore meets the second surface before it can converge. The would-be image lands one R beyond that surface, and so it serves as a virtual object for it, at plus R.
That is the step the entire problem is built around, and it is why a positive object distance appears in a chapter where object distances are almost always negative.
Now the second surface, with one more trap in it. Its radius is minus R, because its centre of curvature is now on the incoming side, back at the centre of the sphere.
Substituting gives one over v equal to two over R, so v is R over two. The beam focuses half a radius beyond the far surface, the standard result for glass of this index.
Advanced level, और यहाँ की ख़ूबसूरती ये है कि पूरा सवाल एक ही idea पर घूमता है, वो image जो कभी बनती ही नहीं, फिर भी object का काम कर सकती है।
Figure में रास्ता देखिए। Beam बाईं ओर से घुसती है, axis की तरफ़ मुड़ती है, और हल्की dashed line दिखाती है कि पहली surface अकेली उसे कहाँ भेजती, गोले से काफ़ी बाहर।
Setup ये है। Radius R और index one point five वाला ठोस glass का गोला हवा में रखा है, और एक parallel beam diameter के साथ चलती है। इसे एक के बाद एक दो single surface refractions मानिए।
पहले surface one. Object अनंत पर है, तो object वाला term ग़ायब हो जाता है और one point five बटा v one बराबर point five बटा R. इससे v one मिलता है तीन R।
यानी पहली surface अपनी image घुसने की जगह से तीन R दाईं ओर बनाना चाहती है। पर दूसरी surface सिर्फ़ दो R दूर है, क्योंकि वो दूरी diameter है।
इसलिए light converge होने से पहले ही दूसरी surface से मिल जाती है। वो बनने वाली image उस surface से एक R आगे गिरती है, और इसलिए उसके लिए virtual object बन जाती है, plus R पर।
पूरा सवाल इसी step पर टिका है, और इसीलिए यहाँ positive object distance दिखता है, उस chapter में जहाँ object distances लगभग हमेशा negative होते हैं।
अब दूसरी surface, जिसमें एक और जाल है। उसका radius minus R है, क्योंकि उसका centre of curvature अब incoming तरफ़ है, गोले के केंद्र पर।
Substitute करने पर one over v बराबर दो बटा R, यानी v बराबर R बटा दो। Beam दूर वाली surface से आधा radius आगे focus होती है, यही standard नतीजा है।

board_events.text: Where these numericals go wrong

board_events.caption: The four traps, and the memory aids that block them

<text x="20" y="26" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Four ways a lens-maker numerical goes wrong</text>

<text x="36" y="84" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">For a biconvex lens R₁ is positive but R₂ is negative. Decide each from where its centre of curvature sits.</text>

<text x="36" y="124" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#b3402f" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">2. Forgetting the medium inside the bracket</text>
<text x="36" y="144" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">The factor is n of the lens over n of the medium, minus one. Any lens-in-liquid problem needs the ratio.</text>

<text x="36" y="204" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">n₁ is where the light starts, n₂ is where it arrives. The image-side index always pairs with v.</text>

<text x="36" y="264" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Refraction relations subtract the object term; the mirror formula adds it. Keep the two structures apart.</text>

<text x="36" y="324" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Refraction subtracts, reflection adds. And the bracket (n − 1) is always hiding the surrounding medium.</text>

board_events.text: Wrong sign for $R_2$, or for $R_1$. For a biconvex lens $R_1$ is positive but $R_2$ is negative. Decide each from where its own centre of curvature sits, every single time.
Forgetting the medium inside the bracket. The factor is really the lens index over the medium index, minus one.
Mixing up $n_1$ and $n_2$ at a single surface. $n_1$ is the medium the light starts in; $n_2$ is the medium it enters. The image-side index always pairs with $v$.
Using the mirror's plus sign. Refraction relations subtract the object term; the mirror formula adds it. Keep the two structures distinct.
Shortcut one: for a symmetric lens use $f = R/2(n-1)$ and skip the sign bookkeeping altogether.
Shortcut two: for any lens in a liquid, compute the ratio directly. The shape cancels, so you never need the radii.
Memory aids: a flat surface is just an infinite radius, and curvature is what focuses. Refraction subtracts, reflection adds. And the bracket always hides the surrounding medium.

segments.text: Before we move to thin lenses proper, here is where these particular numericals go wrong. All four are sign or bookkeeping errors, not conceptual ones.
The board lists them in the order they cost marks, with the memory aids underneath. This is the page to reread the night before the paper.
First and most common: the wrong sign for a radius. For a biconvex lens the first is positive but the second negative. Decide each from where its own centre of curvature sits.
Second: forgetting the medium inside the bracket. The factor written as n minus one is really the lens index divided by the medium index, minus one. Any lens-in-liquid problem needs the full version.
Third: mixing up the two indices at a single surface. The first is where the light starts, the second where it arrives, and the image-side index always pairs with v.
Fourth: importing the mirror's plus sign. The refraction relations subtract the object term, while the mirror formula adds it. Keep the two structures firmly apart in your memory.
Now the two shortcuts. For a symmetric lens, equiconvex or equiconcave, use the focal length as the radius over twice n minus one, and skip the sign bookkeeping altogether.
For any lens dipped in a liquid, compute the ratio of the two focal lengths directly. The shape factor cancels, so you never need the radii and cannot make a radius sign error.

Finally the memory aids. A flat surface is just an infinite radius, and curvature is what focuses. Refraction subtracts while reflection adds. And that innocent bracket is always hiding the surrounding medium.
Thin lenses पर जाने से पहले देख लीजिए कि ये वाले numericals कहाँ बिगड़ते हैं। चारों sign या हिसाब की ग़लतियाँ हैं, concept की नहीं।
Board उन्हें उसी क्रम में गिनाता है जिसमें वो marks खाते हैं, और नीचे memory aids हैं। Paper से पिछली रात यही page दोबारा पढ़िए।
पहली और सबसे आम, radius का ग़लत sign. Biconvex में पहला positive पर दूसरा negative. हर radius का sign उसके अपने centre of curvature से तय कीजिए।
दूसरी, bracket के अंदर medium भूल जाना। जिसे n minus one लिखा जाता है वो असल में lens index बटा medium index, minus one है। हर lens in liquid सवाल पूरा रूप माँगता है।
तीसरी, single surface पर दोनों indices मिला देना। पहला वहाँ का है जहाँ से light चलती है, दूसरा जहाँ पहुँचती है, और image side वाला index हमेशा v के साथ जुड़ता है।
चौथी, mirror वाला plus sign उठा लाना। Refraction के relations object term घटाते हैं, जबकि mirror formula जोड़ता है। दोनों ढाँचे याददाश्त में अलग अलग रखिए।
अब दोनों shortcuts. Symmetric lens के लिए, equiconvex हो या equiconcave, focal length को radius बटा दुगुना n minus one लीजिए, और sign वाला हिसाब पूरा छोड़ दीजिए।
किसी भी liquid में डूबे lens के लिए दोनों focal lengths का ratio सीधे निकालिए। Shape factor cancel हो जाता है, तो radii की ज़रूरत ही नहीं और radius sign की ग़लती मुमकिन ही नहीं।
आख़िर में memory aids. Flat surface बस अनंत radius है, और focus curvature करती है। Refraction घटाता है, reflection जोड़ता है। और वो मासूम सा bracket हमेशा आसपास का medium छिपाए बैठा है।

board_events.text: A convex, converging lens is thicker in the middle. It slows the central part of a wavefront more than the edges.
That curves a flat incoming wave inward, so the rays meet at the focus.
A concave, diverging lens is thinner in the middle and does the reverse, spreading rays apart as though they sprang from a virtual focus.
The magnifying glass, the camera, your spectacles, and the eyepiece of every instrument in this chapter are all lenses doing exactly this.
Everything ahead assumes thin lenses and paraxial rays: narrow beams travelling close to the axis.
Real lenses also suffer chromatic aberration, because $n$, and therefore $f$, depends on wavelength, so different colours focus at slightly different points.
They suffer spherical aberration too. The thin-lens formula ignores both.

segments.text: We have built the lens from two surfaces. Now let us look at what it actually does to the light, because the wave picture makes the behaviour obvious.
The two panels show it. On the left, flat wavefronts leaving a convex lens curved inward. On the right, the same wavefronts leaving a concave lens curved outward.
A convex, converging lens is thicker in the middle. Light travels more slowly in glass, so the central part of a wavefront is held back more than the edges are.
The wave therefore comes out curved inward, and rays, which are always perpendicular to the wavefront, converge to meet at the focus. That is the whole mechanism.
A concave, diverging lens is thinner in the middle and does exactly the reverse. The edges are delayed more, the wave bulges outward, and the rays spread from a virtual focus.
This is not an abstract picture. The magnifying glass, the camera, your spectacles, and the eyepiece of every instrument in the next subtopic are all lenses doing precisely this.
Now the assumptions, which we will keep leaning on. Everything ahead is for thin lenses and paraxial rays, meaning narrow beams travelling close to the principal axis.
Real lenses also suffer chromatic aberration. The refractive index depends on wavelength, so the focal length does too, and different colours come to a focus at slightly different points.
And they suffer spherical aberration, just as wide mirrors did. The thin-lens formula ignores both defects entirely, which is worth remembering when a question mentions either by name.
Lens को हमने दो surfaces से बना लिया। अब देखते हैं कि वो light के साथ असल में करता क्या है, क्योंकि wave वाली तस्वीर से बर्ताव साफ़ हो जाता है।
दोनों panels यही दिखाते हैं। बाईं तरफ़ सपाट wavefronts convex lens से अंदर की तरफ़ मुड़ी निकलती हैं, दाईं तरफ़ वही concave lens से बाहर की तरफ़ मुड़ी।
Convex यानी converging lens बीच में मोटा होता है। Glass में light धीमी चलती है, तो wavefront का बीच वाला हिस्सा किनारों से ज़्यादा रुक जाता है।
इसलिए wave अंदर की तरफ़ मुड़ी हुई निकलती है, और rays, जो हमेशा wavefront के perpendicular होती हैं, focus पर जाकर मिलती हैं। पूरी कार्यविधि यही है।
Concave यानी diverging lens बीच में पतला होता है और बिल्कुल उल्टा करता है। किनारे ज़्यादा रुकते हैं, wave बाहर उभरती है, और rays virtual focus से फैलती हैं।
ये कोई अमूर्त तस्वीर नहीं है। Magnifying glass, camera, आपका चश्मा, और अगले subtopic के हर instrument का eyepiece, सब यही करते हुए lenses हैं।
अब वो assumptions जिन पर हम आगे टिके रहेंगे। आगे का सब कुछ thin lenses और paraxial rays के लिए है, यानी principal axis के पास चलती पतली beams।
असली lenses chromatic aberration से भी जूझते हैं। Refractive index wavelength पर निर्भर है, तो focal length भी, और अलग अलग रंग थोड़े अलग points पर focus होते हैं।
और spherical aberration भी होता है, ठीक जैसे चौड़े mirrors में था। Thin lens formula दोनों दोषों को पूरी तरह नज़रअंदाज़ करता है, और सवाल में इनका नाम आए तो ये याद रखना काम आता है।

<text x="400" y="118" font-size="16" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">1/v + 1/u = 1/f</text>
<text x="400" y="154" font-size="16" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">m = − v / u</text>
<text x="400" y="186" font-size="12.5" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Adds the object term.</text>
<text x="400" y="208" font-size="12.5" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Magnification takes a minus sign.</text>
<rect x="20" y="244" width="700" height="62" rx="6" fill="#22303c"/>
<text x="36" y="268" font-size="13.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Mirror adds, lens subtracts. Both the u term and the sign of m are opposite.</text>
<text x="36" y="292" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">This single confusion is the highest-frequency error in the whole chapter, so fix it now.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Notice the minus sign. The lens formula subtracts the object term; the mirror formula adds it.
And the magnification takes a plus $v/u$ for a lens, against minus $v/u$ for a mirror. Both signs are reversed.
Getting this backwards is the single most common lens mistake in the chapter, and it is worth fixing now rather than in the exam hall.
A negative $m$ still means an inverted, real image; a positive $m$ still means an erect, virtual one. That reading is unchanged.
The sign convention itself is the same New Cartesian one: distances from the optical centre, measured against the incident light for a real object.

segments.text: One relation locates the image through any thin lens, and one sign inside it causes more lost marks than anything else in this chapter.
The board puts the two side by side deliberately. Read across the rows and notice that both differences are sign differences, not structural ones.
Here is the lens formula. One over v minus one over u equals one over f. Say the word minus out loud, because that is the half of it students forget.
The mirror formula added the object term. The lens formula subtracts it. Nothing else about the structure changes, which is precisely why the two are so easy to confuse.
The companion relation is the magnification, and it is the ratio of image height to object height, equal to plus v over u.
For a mirror it was minus v over u. So both signs are reversed between the two devices: the u term in the formula, and the whole magnification.
Getting this backwards is the commonest lens mistake in the chapter. Fix it now, while it costs nothing, rather than in the exam hall where it costs a question.
What does not change is how you read the magnification. A negative value still means an inverted, real image; a positive value still means an erect, virtual one.
And the sign convention is the same New Cartesian one throughout. Distances are measured from the optical centre, and a real object still sits against the incident light, so u stays negative.
एक ही relation किसी भी thin lens की image ढूँढ देता है, और उसके अंदर का एक sign इस chapter में बाक़ी सब से ज़्यादा marks खाता है।
Board ने दोनों को जानबूझकर आमने सामने रखा है। पंक्तियों में पढ़िए और देखिए कि दोनों फ़र्क़ sign के हैं, ढाँचे के नहीं।
ये रहा lens formula. One over v minus one over u बराबर one over f. Minus शब्द ज़ोर से बोलिए, क्योंकि यही आधा हिस्सा students भूलते हैं।
Mirror formula object term जोड़ता था। Lens formula उसे घटाता है। ढाँचे में और कुछ नहीं बदलता, और इसीलिए दोनों में गड़बड़ इतनी आसान है।
साथ चलने वाला relation है magnification, यानी image height बटा object height, जो बराबर है plus v बटा u के।
Mirror में ये minus v बटा u था। तो दोनों devices के बीच दोनों signs उलटे हैं, formula का u वाला term, और पूरा magnification।
इसे उल्टा कर देना chapter की सबसे आम lens ग़लती है। अभी ठीक कर लीजिए, जब कुछ ख़र्च नहीं होता, न कि exam hall में जहाँ सवाल चला जाता है।
जो नहीं बदलता वो है magnification पढ़ने का तरीक़ा। Negative अब भी inverted और real image बताता है, positive अब भी erect और virtual।
और sign convention वही New Cartesian है। दूरियाँ optical centre से नापी जाती हैं, और real object अब भी incident light के उल्टा बैठता है, तो u negative रहता है।

board_events.text: A convex lens behaves like a generous host. Bring an object closer from far away and the real image it throws marches outward and grows.
As the object reaches the focus, the image races off to infinity. That is the projector and searchlight regime.
Step the object inside the focus and the lens switches roles entirely.
It now gives a magnified, erect, virtual image on the same side as the object. That is precisely the magnifying-glass mode.
At exactly $2F$ the image also sits at $2F$, the same size as the object. That is the unit-magnification landmark.
Between $F$ and $2F$ the image forms beyond $2F$, real, inverted and magnified.
Beyond $2F$ the image forms between $F$ and $2F$, real, inverted and diminished, which is the camera regime.

segments.text: A convex lens is not one device but two, and which one you have depends entirely on where the object stands relative to the focus.
The two panels show the extremes. On the left the object sits beyond twice the focal length; on the right it is inside the focus, and the behaviour is unrecognisable.
Think of the convex lens as a generous host. Bring an object closer and closer from far away, and the real image it throws marches outward and grows steadily larger.
Keep going and the growth becomes dramatic. As the object reaches the focus, the image races off toward infinity. That is the projector and searchlight regime.
Now step the object just inside the focus, and the lens switches roles entirely. There is no longer any real image at all to catch on a screen.
Instead it gives a magnified, erect, virtual image on the same side as the object. That is precisely the magnifying-glass mode, the loupe held over a stamp or a fingerprint.
Between those extremes sit the landmarks worth memorising. At exactly twice the focal length, the image also sits at twice the focal length and is the same size as the object.
Between the focus and twice the focus, the image forms beyond twice the focus, real, inverted and magnified. That is the region a projector actually operates in.
And beyond twice the focus, the image forms between the focus and twice the focus, real, inverted and diminished. That is the camera regime, shrinking a large world onto a small sensor.
Convex lens एक device नहीं बल्कि दो हैं, और आपके पास कौन सा है ये पूरी तरह इस पर है कि object focus के मुक़ाबले कहाँ खड़ा है।
दोनों panels दोनों सिरे दिखाते हैं। बाईं तरफ़ object दुगुनी focal length के पार है, दाईं तरफ़ focus के अंदर, और बर्ताव पहचान में ही नहीं आता।
Convex lens को उदार मेज़बान मानिए। Object को दूर से पास लाते जाइए, और वो जो real image फेंकता है वो बाहर की तरफ़ बढ़ती और लगातार बड़ी होती जाती है।
चलते रहिए और बढ़ना नाटकीय हो जाता है। Object focus पर पहुँचते ही image अनंत की तरफ़ भाग जाती है। यही projector वाला इलाक़ा है।
अब object को focus के ज़रा सा अंदर कर दीजिए, और lens अपनी भूमिका पूरी तरह बदल देता है। अब screen पर पकड़ने लायक़ कोई real image बचती ही नहीं।
उसकी जगह वो object की ही तरफ़ एक magnified, erect और virtual image देता है। यही magnifying glass वाला रूप है, वही loupe जो डाक टिकट या उँगली के निशान पर रखा जाता है।
इन दोनों सिरों के बीच याद रखने लायक़ landmarks हैं। ठीक दुगुनी focal length पर image भी दुगुनी focal length पर बनती है और object के बराबर आकार की होती है।
Focus और दुगुने focus के बीच object हो तो image दुगुने focus के पार बनती है, real, inverted और magnified. Projector असल में इसी इलाक़े में चलता है।
और दुगुने focus के पार object हो तो image focus और दुगुने focus के बीच बनती है, real, inverted और diminished. यही camera वाला इलाक़ा है, बड़ी दुनिया को छोटे sensor पर सिकोड़ता हुआ।

board_events.text: A concave lens is utterly predictable. For any real object it always produces a virtual, erect, diminished image.
That image always forms between the lens and the focus, on the same side as the object.
It is the exact analogue of a convex mirror, which behaved the same way for every real object.
