board_events.text: A thin crown prism of apex angle $5^{\circ}$ has $n_v = 1.524$, $n_r = 1.514$ and $n_y = 1.519$. Find the mean deviation, the angular dispersion and the dispersive power.
So the mean deviation is about 2.6 degrees, the colour spread only 0.05 degrees, and the dispersive power about 0.019.
Note the ratio: dispersion is roughly one part in fifty of the deviation. That small number is why single lenses show only faint colour fringing.

segments.text: Now a main-level calculation that ties the three dispersion quantities together in one problem: mean deviation, angular dispersion and dispersive power, all from the same three indices.
The figure lays out the three indices and the arithmetic. Notice we work in the thin-prism limit throughout, so every deviation is just index-minus-one times the apex angle.
The question. A thin crown prism of apex angle five degrees has a violet index of one point five two four, a red index of one point five one four, and a yellow index of one point five one nine.
First the mean deviation, taken at the yellow line. It is the yellow index minus one, times the apex angle: nought point five one nine times five degrees, which is two point five nine five degrees.
Then the angular dispersion, the spread between violet and red. It is the index difference, nought point zero one, times the apex angle, giving nought point zero five degrees.

Finally the dispersive power, the ratio of the two. It is the index difference over the yellow index minus one, that is nought point zero one over nought point five one nine, about nought point zero one nine.
So the numbers tell a clear story. The mean deviation is about two point six degrees, the colour spread only nought point zero five degrees, and the dispersive power about nought point zero one nine.

Read the ratio it hides. The dispersion is roughly one part in fifty of the deviation. That small number is exactly why an ordinary single lens shows only faint colour fringing, not a full spectrum, at its edges.
अब एक main level हिसाब जो तीनों dispersion राशियों को एक सवाल में जोड़ता है, mean deviation, angular dispersion और dispersive power, सब उन्हीं तीन indices से।
Figure तीनों indices और arithmetic सामने रखती है। ध्यान दीजिए हम पूरे वक़्त thin prism limit में काम करते हैं, तो हर deviation बस index minus one गुणा apex angle है।
सवाल ये है। पाँच degrees apex angle वाले thin crown prism का violet index one point five two four, red index one point five one four, और yellow index one point five one nine है।
पहले mean deviation, yellow line पर लिया। वो yellow index minus one, गुणा apex angle है, शून्य point five one nine गुणा पाँच degrees, जो है two point five nine five degrees।
फिर angular dispersion, violet और red के बीच का फैलाव। वो index का अंतर, शून्य point zero one, गुणा apex angle है, जो देता है शून्य point zero five degrees।
आख़िर में dispersive power, दोनों का ratio. वो index अंतर बटा yellow index minus one है, यानी शून्य point zero one बटा शून्य point five one nine, लगभग शून्य point zero one nine।
तो numbers साफ़ कहानी कहते हैं। Mean deviation लगभग दो point छह degrees, रंग का फैलाव सिर्फ़ शून्य point zero five degrees, और dispersive power लगभग शून्य point zero one nine।
इसमें छिपा ratio पढ़िए। Dispersion, deviation का लगभग पचास में एक हिस्सा है। वही छोटा number है जिसकी वजह से साधारण अकेला lens अपने किनारों पर बस हल्की रंग की झालर दिखाता है, पूरा spectrum नहीं।

board_events.text: For a prism of refractive index 1.5, find the largest apex angle from which a ray can still emerge from the second face.
For emergence, the second-face angle $r_2$ must not exceed the critical angle $C$. Since $r_1 + r_2 = A$, the apex angle is largest when both internal angles equal $C$.
Beyond about 83.6 degrees, the ray strikes the second face beyond the critical angle and is totally internally reflected, never leaving the glass.
This is why steep prisms are used as reflectors, not refractors. The same total internal reflection that traps the ray here is what makes a 45-degree prism a perfect mirror.
It also explains the sixty-degree standard: a comfortable margin below the trapping limit.

segments.text: Advanced level to finish the numericals, and this one connects the prism straight back to total internal reflection from the last part of the chapter.
The figure shows the limiting case, where both internal angles have grown to exactly the critical angle at the same time. Push the apex any wider and the light can no longer escape.
The question. For a prism of refractive index one point five, find the largest apex angle from which a ray can still emerge from the second face.

Set up the condition. For the ray to emerge, its second-face angle must not exceed the critical angle. Since the two internal angles sum to the apex, the apex is largest when both equal the critical angle.
First find the critical angle. Its sine is one over the index, one over one point five, that is nought point six six seven, giving about forty one point eight degrees.
The maximum apex angle is then twice that, about eighty three point six degrees. That is the steepest prism of this glass from which any light can emerge.
Read the physics. Beyond about eighty three point six degrees, the ray strikes the second face beyond the critical angle and is totally internally reflected, so it never leaves the glass at all.
This is why steep prisms are used as reflectors, not refractors. The same total internal reflection that traps the ray here makes a forty five degree prism a perfect, loss-free mirror.
And it explains the sixty-degree standard once more. Sixty degrees sits comfortably below the eighty three degree trapping limit, giving a reliable margin so the light always gets out the far side.
Numericals ख़त्म करने के लिए advanced level, और ये prism को सीधे chapter के पिछले हिस्से वाले total internal reflection से जोड़ता है।
Figure limiting case दिखाती है, जहाँ दोनों internal angles एक साथ ठीक critical angle तक बढ़ गए हैं। Apex ज़रा भी चौड़ा कीजिए और रोशनी निकल ही नहीं सकती।
सवाल ये है। One point five refractive index वाले prism के लिए, सबसे बड़ा apex angle निकालिए जिससे ray अब भी दूसरी face से निकल सके।
Condition बनाइए। निकलने के लिए दूसरी face पर कोण critical angle से ऊपर न जाए। दोनों internal angles apex में जुड़ते हैं, तो apex सबसे बड़ा तब जब दोनों critical angle के बराबर हों।
पहले critical angle निकालिए। उसका sine है एक बटा index, एक बटा one point five, यानी शून्य point six six seven, जो देता है लगभग इकतालीस point आठ degrees।
अधिकतम apex angle फिर उसका दुगुना है, लगभग तिरासी point छह degrees. यही इस glass का सबसे तीखा prism है जिससे कोई रोशनी निकल सके।
Physics पढ़िए। लगभग तिरासी point छह degrees के आगे, ray दूसरी face से critical angle के पार टकराती है और पूरी तरह अंदर ही परावर्तित हो जाती है, तो वो glass से निकलती ही नहीं।

इसीलिए तीखे prisms reflectors की तरह इस्तेमाल होते हैं, refractors नहीं। वही total internal reflection जो यहाँ ray फँसाता है, वही पैंतालीस degree वाले prism को perfect, बिना loss वाला mirror बनाता है।
और ये साठ degree वाला standard एक बार फिर समझा देता है। साठ degrees तिरासी degree वाली trapping limit से आराम से नीचे बैठता है, एक भरोसेमंद margin देता है ताकि रोशनी हमेशा दूसरी तरफ़ निकल जाए।

board_events.text: Using the prism formula away from minimum deviation. $n = \sin((A+\delta_m)/2)/\sin(A/2)$ holds only at $\delta_m$. For any other $\delta$, use $r_1+r_2=A$ with Snell at each face.
Confusing dispersion with deviation. Deviation is the average bend $(n-1)A$; dispersion is the spread $(n_v-n_r)A$. Dispersive power is their ratio.
Forgetting $A_{\max}=2C$. If the apex angle exceeds twice the critical angle, no ray emerges at all; the second face totally internally reflects it.
Reversing the rainbow colours. Primary bow: red on the outside. Secondary bow: red on the inside. The extra reflection flips the order and dims the bow.
Reflex one: for a thin prism, deviation is simply $(n-1)A$, no incidence angle needed.
Reflex two: violet bends most, red least, because short wavelengths have the larger index. And both the blue sky and the red sunset come from Rayleigh's one-over-lambda-to-the-fourth law.
Memory aids: the prism formula is a minimum-deviation-only tool; deviation is the average, dispersion the spread; and Violet Bends Most.

segments.text: To close the subtopic, here is where prism and dispersion marks actually leak. All four are confusions of one relation for another, easily avoided once named.
The board lists them in the order they cost marks, with the memory aids underneath. Reread this page the night before the paper.

First, using the prism formula away from minimum deviation. It holds only at the symmetric passage. For any other incidence angle, return to the general relations, the internal angles summing to the apex, with Snell at each face.

Second, confusing dispersion with deviation. Deviation is the average bend of the beam, index-minus-one times the apex angle. Dispersion is the spread between colours, the index difference times the apex angle. Dispersive power is their ratio.
Third, forgetting the maximum apex angle. If the apex exceeds twice the critical angle, no ray emerges at all; the second face totally internally reflects it back into the glass.
Fourth, reversing the rainbow colours. The primary bow has red on the outside; the secondary bow has red on the inside. The extra internal reflection both flips the order and dims the bow.
Now the reflexes. For a thin prism the deviation is simply index-minus-one times the apex angle, with no incidence angle needed. That one relation carries most dispersion problems.

The second reflex is qualitative. Violet bends most, red least, because the shorter wavelength has the larger index. And both the blue sky and the red sunset are Rayleigh's one-over-wavelength-to-the-fourth law.
Finally the memory aids. The prism formula is a minimum-deviation-only tool. Deviation is the average, dispersion is the spread. And Violet Bends Most, three words that fix the whole colour order.
Subtopic बंद करने के लिए, यहाँ prism और dispersion के marks असल में रिसते हैं। चारों एक relation को दूसरे से भ्रमित करना हैं, नाम पड़ते ही टल जाते हैं।
Board उन्हें उसी क्रम में गिनाता है जिसमें वो marks खाते हैं, नीचे memory aids हैं। Paper से पिछली रात यही page दोबारा पढ़िए।

पहला, prism formula को minimum deviation से हटकर इस्तेमाल करना। वो सिर्फ़ symmetric passage पर चलता है। किसी और incidence angle के लिए general relations पर लौटिए, internal angles apex में जुड़ते, हर face पर Snell के साथ।

दूसरा, dispersion को deviation से भ्रमित करना। Deviation beam का औसत मोड़ है, index minus one गुणा apex angle. Dispersion रंगों के बीच फैलाव है, index अंतर गुणा apex angle. Dispersive power दोनों का ratio है।
तीसरा, अधिकतम apex angle भूलना। Apex critical angle के दुगुने से ऊपर हो तो कोई ray निकलती ही नहीं, दूसरी face उसे पूरी तरह अंदर ही परावर्तित कर देती है।
चौथा, rainbow के रंग उलट देना। Primary bow में red बाहर है, secondary bow में red अंदर। वो अतिरिक्त internal reflection क्रम भी उलटता है और bow को धुँधला भी करता है।
अब reflexes. Thin prism के लिए deviation बस index minus one गुणा apex angle है, कोई incidence angle नहीं चाहिए। वही एक relation ज़्यादातर dispersion सवाल निपटा देता है।

दूसरा reflex qualitative है। Violet सबसे ज़्यादा, red सबसे कम मुड़ता है, क्योंकि छोटी wavelength का index बड़ा है। और नीला आसमान तथा लाल सूर्यास्त दोनों Rayleigh के one over wavelength to the fourth नियम से हैं।
आख़िर में memory aids. Prism formula सिर्फ़ minimum deviation का औज़ार है। Deviation औसत है, dispersion फैलाव। और Violet Bends Most, तीन शब्द जो पूरा रंग क्रम पक्का कर देते हैं।

board_events.text: An optical instrument cannot make an object bigger. What it does is make the object subtend a larger angle at your eye.
How large something looks is set by the angle its image subtends on your retina, not by its true size or distance.
Magnifying power is that angular ratio: the angle with the instrument divided by the angle without it. It is an angular magnification, not a size ratio.
Here $\beta$ is the angle the final image subtends with the instrument, and $\alpha$ the angle the object subtends at the naked eye.
The Moon is huge but far, so it subtends a small angle and looks small. A telescope enlarges that angle, and the Moon looks close.
Keeping this straight, angle not size, prevents nearly every conceptual error in this subtopic.

segments.text: The last subtopic of the chapter is about the instruments that put everything so far to work: microscopes and telescopes. But first we need to be precise about what they actually do.
The figure shows the starting point. A distant object sends rays to your eye that spread only slightly, so the object subtends a small angle and therefore looks small.
Here is the key idea. An optical instrument cannot make an object physically bigger. What it does instead is make the object subtend a larger angle at your eye.
That matters because of how vision works. How large something looks is set entirely by the angle its image subtends on your retina, not by the object's true size or its distance from you.
So magnifying power is an angular ratio: the angle the image subtends with the instrument, over the angle the object subtends without it. It is an angular magnification, never a size ratio.
In symbols, the magnifying power is beta over alpha, and holding those two angles clearly apart is the whole discipline of this subtopic.
Beta is the angle the final image subtends when you look through the instrument. Alpha is the angle the bare object subtends at your naked eye, viewed in the most favourable ordinary way.
Think of the Moon. It is enormous but far, so it subtends a small angle and looks small. A telescope enlarges that angle, and the Moon looks close enough to touch.
Keeping this one distinction straight, angle and not size, prevents nearly every conceptual error you can make in this subtopic. The object never grows; only its image on your retina does.
Chapter का आख़िरी subtopic उन instruments के बारे में है जो अब तक की हर चीज़ को काम पर लगाते हैं, microscopes और telescopes. पर पहले हमें ठीक ठीक समझना होगा कि वो करते क्या हैं।
Figure शुरुआती बिंदु दिखाती है। दूर की object आपकी आँख तक ऐसी rays भेजती है जो बहुत थोड़ा फैलती हैं, इसलिए object छोटा कोण बनाती है और छोटी दिखती है।
यही असली idea है। कोई optical instrument object को शारीरिक रूप से बड़ा नहीं कर सकता। वो इसके बजाय object को आपकी आँख पर बड़ा कोण बनवाता है।
ये इसलिए मायने रखता है क्योंकि दृष्टि ऐसे ही काम करती है। कोई चीज़ कितनी बड़ी दिखती है ये पूरी तरह इस कोण से तय होता है जो उसकी image आपके retina पर बनाती है, object के असली आकार या दूरी से नहीं।
तो magnifying power एक कोणीय अनुपात है, instrument के साथ image का कोण बटा उसके बिना object का कोण। ये angular magnification है, कभी size ratio नहीं।
Symbols में magnifying power है beta बटा alpha, और उन दोनों कोणों को साफ़ अलग रखना ही इस subtopic का पूरा अनुशासन है।
Beta वो कोण है जो final image बनाती है जब आप instrument से देखते हैं। Alpha वो कोण है जो नंगी object आपकी नंगी आँख पर बनाती है, सबसे अनुकूल साधारण तरीक़े से देखी गई।
Moon के बारे में सोचिए। वो विशाल पर दूर है, इसलिए छोटा कोण बनाता है और छोटा दिखता है। Telescope उस कोण को बड़ा करता है, और Moon इतना पास दिखता है कि छू लें।
यही एक फ़र्क़ साफ़ रखना, कोण और आकार नहीं, इस subtopic की लगभग हर conceptual ग़लती रोक देता है। Object कभी बड़ी नहीं होती, सिर्फ़ आपके retina पर उसकी image होती है।

board_events.text: The simplest instrument is a single convex lens held so the object sits just inside its focus. This is the magnifying glass.
The lens then forms an enlarged, erect, virtual image, which the eye views comfortably.
The near point, the closest distance the eye can focus without strain, is taken as 25 cm for a normal eye and written $D$.
The near-point setting gives one extra unit of magnification, at the cost of some eye strain.
So a shorter focal length gives a stronger magnifier. The wording of a question, relaxed or near point, tells you which formula to use.

segments.text: Start with the simplest instrument of all, the one you have already used: a single convex lens working as a magnifying glass.
The figure shows the arrangement. Hold the lens so the object sits just inside its focus, and it behaves in exactly the magnifying-glass mode we met when studying convex lenses.
The simplest instrument is a single convex lens held so the object sits just inside its focus. There is nothing more to a simple microscope than that.
The lens then forms an enlarged, erect, virtual image on the same side as the object. The eye views that image comfortably, and it looks much larger than the object seen alone.
One number sets the standard. The near point is the closest distance at which the eye can focus without strain, taken as twenty five centimetres for a normal eye and written as capital D throughout.
Now the two magnifying powers, depending on where the final image sits. With a relaxed eye, the image is at infinity, and the magnifying power is simply D over f.
With the eye strained to place the image at the near point instead, you gain a little. The magnifying power becomes one plus D over f.
So the near-point setting buys exactly one extra unit of magnification, at the cost of some eye strain. That is the trade-off between the relaxed and the strained viewing.
The lesson is that a shorter focal length gives a stronger magnifier. And the wording of a question, relaxed or near point, tells you at once which of the two formulas to reach for.
सबसे सरल instrument से शुरू कीजिए, वो जो आप पहले भी इस्तेमाल कर चुके हैं, एक अकेला convex lens जो magnifying glass की तरह काम करता है।
Figure व्यवस्था दिखाती है। Lens को ऐसे पकड़िए कि object उसके focus के ज़रा अंदर बैठे, और वो ठीक उसी magnifying glass वाले रूप में बर्ताव करता है जो convex lenses पढ़ते वक़्त मिला था।
सबसे सरल instrument एक अकेला convex lens है जो ऐसे पकड़ा जाए कि object उसके focus के ज़रा अंदर हो। Simple microscope इससे ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं।
Lens फिर object की ही तरफ़ एक बड़ी, सीधी, virtual image बनाता है। आँख उस image को आराम से देखती है, और वो अकेली object से कहीं बड़ी दिखती है।
एक number standard तय करता है। Near point वो सबसे पास की दूरी है जिस पर आँख बिना ज़ोर डाले focus कर सकती है, सामान्य आँख के लिए पच्चीस centimetre मानी जाती है और पूरे वक़्त capital D लिखी जाती है।
अब दोनों magnifying powers, इस पर कि final image कहाँ बैठती है। आराम में आँख के साथ image अनंत पर होती है, और magnifying power बस D बटा f होती है।
आँख को ज़ोर देकर image को near point पर रखने पर थोड़ा फ़ायदा मिलता है। Magnifying power बन जाती है one plus D बटा f।
तो near point वाली setting ठीक एक अतिरिक्त इकाई magnification देती है, कुछ आँख के तनाव की क़ीमत पर। यही relaxed और strained देखने के बीच का सौदा है।
सबक़ ये है कि छोटी focal length ज़्यादा ताक़तवर magnifier देती है। और सवाल के शब्द, relaxed या near point, तुरंत बता देते हैं कि दोनों में से कौन सा formula उठाना है।

board_events.text: A single lens can only magnify so far before aberrations spoil the image. The compound microscope splits the job across two lenses.
The objective, of short focal length, sits close to the object and forms a real, enlarged, inverted image inside the tube.
The eyepiece then works as a simple microscope on that intermediate image, magnifying it a second time.
The two stages multiply. The total magnification is the objective's linear magnification times the eyepiece's angular magnification.
For high power you want both focal lengths short, so both stages contribute strongly.
The image you finally see is inverted, which does not matter for a cell on a slide.

segments.text: A single lens can only be pushed so far. Beyond a modest magnification its aberrations ruin the image, so the compound microscope does the job in two stages instead.
The figure shows the two-lens layout. The objective near the object, the eyepiece near the eye, and a real intermediate image formed between them inside the tube.
The idea is division of labour. Rather than ask one lens to do everything, we split the magnification across two lenses in series, each doing a manageable share.
The objective comes first. It has a short focal length, sits close to the object, and forms a real, enlarged, inverted image partway up the tube.
The eyepiece then takes over. It works exactly as a simple microscope, treating that real intermediate image as its object and magnifying it a second time for the eye.
Because the stages act in series, their magnifications multiply. The total is the objective's linear magnification times the eyepiece's angular magnification, never their sum.
Writing it out: the objective contributes the image distance over the object distance, and the eyepiece contributes D over its focal length, at the near-point setting.
So for high power you want both focal lengths short. A short objective focal length gives a large first-stage magnification, and a short eyepiece focal length gives a large second-stage one.
The image you finally see is inverted, because each stage or the objective flips it. For looking at a cell on a slide that inversion does not matter in the slightest.
एक अकेला lens एक हद तक ही ले जाया जा सकता है। मामूली magnification के आगे उसके aberrations image बिगाड़ देते हैं, इसलिए compound microscope यही काम दो चरणों में करता है।
Figure दो lens वाली व्यवस्था दिखाती है। Objective object के पास, eyepiece आँख के पास, और उनके बीच tube के अंदर बनती एक real intermediate image।
Idea है काम का बँटवारा। एक lens से सब कुछ कराने के बजाय, हम magnification को शृंखला में दो lenses पर बाँट देते हैं, हर एक संभालने लायक़ हिस्सा करता है।
पहले objective आता है। उसकी focal length छोटी होती है, वो object के पास बैठता है, और tube में आधे रास्ते एक real, बड़ी, उलटी image बनाता है।
फिर eyepiece संभाल लेता है। वो बिल्कुल simple microscope की तरह काम करता है, उस real intermediate image को अपनी object मानकर आँख के लिए दूसरी बार बड़ा करता है।
क्योंकि चरण शृंखला में काम करते हैं, उनके magnifications गुणा होते हैं। कुल है objective का linear magnification गुणा eyepiece का angular magnification, कभी उनका जोड़ नहीं।
पूरा लिखिए तो, objective देता है image distance बटा object distance, और eyepiece देता है D बटा अपनी focal length, near point setting पर।
तो ऊँची power के लिए आप दोनों focal lengths छोटी चाहते हैं। छोटी objective focal length बड़ा पहला चरण magnification देती है, और छोटी eyepiece focal length बड़ा दूसरा।
जो image आप आख़िर में देखते हैं वो उलटी होती है, क्योंकि objective उसे पलट देता है। Slide पर रखी किसी cell को देखने के लिए वो उलटापन ज़रा भी मायने नहीं रखता।

board_events.text: A telescope solves the opposite problem to a microscope: large objects made small by great distance, rather than small objects nearby.
The object is effectively at infinity, so parallel rays enter and the objective brings them to a focus at its focal plane.
In normal adjustment the eyepiece's focus coincides with the objective's, so the final rays leave parallel and the relaxed eye views an image at infinity.
The magnifying power is the ratio of the focal lengths, and the tube length is their sum.
So a telescope wants a long objective focal length and a short eyepiece, the reverse of what a microscope wants.
The image is inverted, which is why astronomical telescopes show an upside-down Moon.

segments.text: The telescope solves the mirror-image problem to the microscope. Instead of small objects nearby, it deals with large objects made small by their enormous distance.
The figure shows the essential path. Parallel rays arrive from a distant star, the objective brings them to a focus, and the eyepiece sends them out parallel again to the eye.
Because the object is effectively at infinity, the light from any one point on it is a bundle of parallel rays, and the objective brings each bundle to a point in its focal plane.
That focal plane holds a small, real, inverted image of the distant object, formed right where the objective's focal length ends. The eyepiece then examines it.
The standard setting is normal adjustment: the eyepiece's focus coincides with the objective's, so the final rays leave parallel and the relaxed eye sees an image at infinity.
In that setting the two key relations are simple. The magnifying power is the objective focal length over the eyepiece focal length, and the tube length is the sum of the two focal lengths.
Read the magnifying power carefully, because it is the reverse of the microscope. Here you want a long objective focal length on top and a short eyepiece focal length below.
So the design goals are opposite. A microscope wants both focal lengths short; a telescope wants a long objective and a short eyepiece. Confusing the two is a classic error.
And the final image is inverted, which is why an astronomical telescope shows the Moon upside down. For a star that is invisible, and for the Moon astronomers simply do not mind.
Telescope microscope का दर्पण-प्रतिबिंब सवाल हल करता है। पास की छोटी objects के बजाय, वो उन बड़ी objects से निपटता है जो अपनी भारी दूरी से छोटी हो गई हैं।
Figure असली रास्ता दिखाती है। दूर के तारे से parallel rays आती हैं, objective उन्हें focus करता है, और eyepiece उन्हें फिर parallel करके आँख की तरफ़ भेज देता है।
क्योंकि object अनंत पर है, उसके एक बिंदु से आती रोशनी parallel rays का गुच्छा है, और objective हर गुच्छे को अपने focal plane में एक बिंदु पर ले आता है।
वो focal plane दूर की object की एक छोटी, real, उलटी image रखता है, ठीक वहाँ बनी जहाँ objective की focal length ख़त्म होती है। फिर eyepiece उसे देखता है।
Standard setting है normal adjustment, जहाँ eyepiece का focus objective के focus पर होता है, तो final rays parallel निकलती हैं और आराम में आँख अनंत पर image देखती है।
उस setting में दोनों मुख्य relations सरल हैं। Magnifying power है objective focal length बटा eyepiece focal length, और tube length दोनों focal lengths का जोड़।
Magnifying power को ध्यान से पढ़िए, क्योंकि ये microscope का उल्टा है। यहाँ आप ऊपर लंबी objective focal length और नीचे छोटी eyepiece focal length चाहते हैं।
तो design के लक्ष्य उल्टे हैं। Microscope दोनों focal lengths छोटी चाहता है, telescope लंबी objective और छोटी eyepiece. दोनों को मिला देना classic ग़लती है।
और final image उलटी होती है, इसीलिए astronomical telescope Moon को उल्टा दिखाता है। तारे के लिए वो अदृश्य है, और Moon के लिए astronomers बस बुरा नहीं मानते।

board_events.text: For large telescopes a mirror replaces the objective lens, and the advantages are decisive.
A mirror has no chromatic aberration, because it bends every colour identically. A lens always splits colours slightly.
A mirror is also cheaper and lighter, needs only one surface ground, and can be supported across its whole back so it does not sag under its own weight.
A large aperture also gathers more light, making faint, distant objects visible. Every research observatory today uses a reflector.

board_events.text: The astronomical telescope's inverted image is useless for viewing on land. A terrestrial telescope inserts a third lens to re-invert it.
That erecting lens turns the image upright without changing the magnification, at the cost of a longer tube.

segments.text: Two practical variations complete the telescope story: using a mirror instead of a lens, and turning the image the right way up for use on Earth.

The first figure shows a reflecting telescope. A large concave mirror replaces the objective lens, gathering the light and forming the image, with a small secondary mirror directing it to the eyepiece.
For any large telescope, a mirror objective wins decisively over a lens, and it is worth knowing exactly why, because examiners ask for the reasons directly.
The first reason is colour. A mirror has no chromatic aberration, because reflection bends every colour equally. A lens always splits the colours a little, blurring the image.
The mirror is also cheaper and lighter, since only one surface is ground, and it can be supported across its whole back, so it does not sag under its weight the way a huge lens would.

And a large mirror aperture gathers far more light, which makes faint and distant objects visible at all. For all these reasons, every serious research observatory today uses a reflector, not a refractor.
Now the second variation, shown in the lower figure. The astronomical telescope gives an inverted image, which is perfectly fine for stars but useless for looking at something on land.
The fix is a terrestrial telescope, which inserts a third lens between the objective and the eyepiece. That extra lens re-inverts the intermediate image, so the final view comes out the right way up.
This erecting lens turns the image upright without changing the magnifying power at all. The only cost is a longer tube, which is why terrestrial telescopes and old spyglasses are so noticeably long.
दो व्यावहारिक रूप telescope की कहानी पूरी करते हैं, lens के बजाय mirror इस्तेमाल करना, और image को धरती पर काम के लिए सीधा करना।
पहली figure एक reflecting telescope दिखाती है। एक बड़ा concave mirror objective lens की जगह लेता है, रोशनी इकट्ठी करके image बनाता है, और एक छोटा secondary mirror उसे eyepiece की तरफ़ मोड़ता है।
किसी भी बड़े telescope के लिए mirror objective, lens पर साफ़ जीतता है, और ठीक क्यों, ये जानना ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि examiners वजहें सीधे पूछते हैं।
पहली वजह रंग है। Mirror में chromatic aberration नहीं होता, क्योंकि reflection हर रंग को बराबर मोड़ता है। Lens रंगों को थोड़ा बाँट देता है, image धुँधली कर देता है।
Mirror सस्ता और हल्का भी है, क्योंकि सिर्फ़ एक surface घिसनी पड़ती है, और उसे पूरे पीछे से सहारा मिलता है, तो वो अपने वज़न से नहीं झुकता जैसे विशाल lens झुकता।

और बड़ा mirror aperture कहीं ज़्यादा रोशनी बटोरता है, जो धुँधली और दूर की objects को दिखने ही लायक़ बनाता है। इन्हीं वजहों से आज हर गंभीर research observatory reflector इस्तेमाल करती है, refractor नहीं।
अब दूसरा रूप, नीचे वाली figure में। Astronomical telescope उलटी image देता है, जो तारों के लिए बिल्कुल ठीक है पर धरती पर कुछ देखने के लिए बेकार।
उपाय है terrestrial telescope, जो objective और eyepiece के बीच एक तीसरा lens डाल देता है। वो अतिरिक्त lens intermediate image को फिर उलट देता है, तो final नज़ारा सीधा आता है।
वो erecting lens image को सीधा करता है बिना magnifying power ज़रा भी बदले। एकमात्र क़ीमत लंबा tube है, इसीलिए terrestrial telescopes और पुराने spyglasses इतने ध्यान खींचते ढंग से लंबे होते हैं।

board_events.text: In normal adjustment the objective and eyepiece share a focal point, where the real intermediate image of height $h$ forms.
The object at infinity subtends angle $\alpha$ at the objective. That same angle reaches the eye when no instrument is used, so $\alpha$ is the naked-eye angle.
The eyepiece then presents the intermediate image at angle $\beta$ to the relaxed eye, with the image at its focus.
The image height cancels, leaving the clean ratio of focal lengths. And since power is one over focal length, equivalently $M = P_e/P_o$.

segments.text: The telescope magnifying power has a short, clean derivation that boards ask for directly, and it rests entirely on the two angles subtended at a shared intermediate image.
The figure holds the whole argument. The real intermediate image sits at the common focus, its height h subtending one angle back at the objective and another forward at the eyepiece.
Set it up. In normal adjustment the objective and the eyepiece share a single focal point, and that is exactly where the real intermediate image, of height h, is formed.
First the naked-eye angle. The object at infinity subtends alpha at the objective, and because it is so far, that same angle reaches the eye with no instrument at all.
From the geometry, that angle alpha is the image height h divided by the objective focal length, since the image sits one objective-focal-length behind the objective.
Now the angle through the instrument. The eyepiece presents that same intermediate image to the relaxed eye, with the image at the eyepiece's own focus, subtending a larger angle beta.
And that angle beta is the same height h divided by the eyepiece focal length, because now the image sits one eyepiece-focal-length in front of the eyepiece.
Take the ratio, which is the magnifying power. The height h cancels top and bottom, and what survives is beautifully clean: the objective focal length over the eyepiece focal length.
One extra form is worth carrying. Since power is one over focal length, the same result reads as the eyepiece power over the objective power, eyepiece on top. Note the inversion.
Telescope की magnifying power की एक छोटी, साफ़ derivation है जो boards सीधे पूछते हैं, और वो पूरी तरह एक साझा intermediate image पर बने दो कोणों पर टिकी है।
Figure में पूरा तर्क है। Real intermediate image साझा focus पर बैठी है, उसकी ऊँचाई h पीछे objective पर एक कोण और आगे eyepiece पर दूसरा कोण बनाती है।
Setup बनाइए। Normal adjustment में objective और eyepiece एक ही focal point साझा करते हैं, और ठीक वहीं ऊँचाई h वाली real intermediate image बनती है।
पहले नंगी आँख वाला कोण। अनंत पर object objective पर alpha बनाती है, और इतनी दूर होने से बिना instrument के आँख तक वही कोण पहुँचता है।
Geometry से वो कोण alpha है image ऊँचाई h बटा objective focal length, क्योंकि image objective के पीछे एक objective focal length पर बैठी है।
अब instrument के ज़रिए कोण। Eyepiece वही intermediate image आराम में आँख को दिखाता है, image eyepiece के अपने focus पर, एक बड़ा कोण beta बनाते हुए।
और वो कोण beta है वही ऊँचाई h बटा eyepiece focal length, क्योंकि अब image eyepiece के आगे एक eyepiece focal length पर बैठी है।
अनुपात लीजिए, जो magnifying power है। ऊँचाई h ऊपर नीचे cancel हो जाती है, और जो बचता है वो ख़ूबसूरती से साफ़ है, objective focal length बटा eyepiece focal length।
एक अतिरिक्त रूप साथ रखने लायक़ है। Power एक बटा focal length है, तो वही नतीजा है eyepiece power बटा objective power, eyepiece ऊपर। उस उलटाव पर ध्यान दीजिए।

sections.title: Microscope versus telescope, and the human eye

board_events.text: Two designs, opposite goals

board_events.caption: The microscope and telescope compared side by side

board_events.text: The two instruments look similar, two lenses in a tube, but their design goals are opposite, and keeping them apart prevents most errors.
A microscope views small, near objects; a telescope views large, distant ones. That difference drives everything else.
A microscope wants both focal lengths short. A telescope wants a long objective and a short eyepiece.
The magnifications differ too: the microscope multiplies two stages, $m_o \times M_e$, while the telescope takes the ratio $f_o/f_e$.
The eye itself is the final instrument in every chain. Its lens focuses images onto the retina, adjusting focal length by changing shape, a process called accommodation.
A near point that recedes with age is why reading glasses become common; a near-sighted or far-sighted eye is corrected with a diverging or converging lens.
Every instrument in this subtopic ultimately hands its image to this one remarkable lens.

segments.text: To close the concept run, a direct comparison of the two instruments, and a look at the lens that sits at the end of every optical chain: the human eye.
The board sets the microscope and telescope side by side. They look almost identical, two lenses in a tube, but their purposes, and therefore their designs, are opposite.
The instruments look similar but solve opposite problems, and keeping that opposition clear in your mind prevents the majority of errors students make in this subtopic.
Start with purpose. A microscope views small objects placed close to it; a telescope views large objects at enormous distances. Every design choice flows from that single difference.
So the focal-length recipes are opposite. A microscope wants both focal lengths short, to magnify strongly at both stages. A telescope wants a long objective and a short eyepiece.
The magnification formulas differ too. The microscope multiplies two stages, objective linear times eyepiece angular. The telescope simply takes the ratio of the two focal lengths.
Now the eye, the final instrument in every chain. Its own lens focuses images onto the retina, and it adjusts its focal length by changing its shape, a process called accommodation.
This explains familiar things. A near point that recedes with age is why reading glasses become common. And a short-sighted or long-sighted eye is corrected with a diverging or converging lens.
So every instrument in this subtopic ultimately hands its image to this one remarkable lens. The microscope and telescope only prepare the light; the eye does the final focusing onto the retina.
Concept वाले हिस्से को बंद करने के लिए, दोनों instruments की सीधी तुलना, और उस lens पर एक नज़र जो हर optical शृंखला के आख़िर में बैठा है, मानव आँख।
Board microscope और telescope को आमने सामने रखता है। वो लगभग एक जैसे दिखते हैं, tube में दो lenses, पर उनके मक़सद, और इसलिए designs, उल्टे हैं।
Instruments एक जैसे दिखते हैं पर उल्टे सवाल हल करते हैं, और उस उलटाव को मन में साफ़ रखना students की इस subtopic की ज़्यादातर ग़लतियाँ रोक देता है।
मक़सद से शुरू कीजिए। Microscope अपने पास रखी छोटी objects देखता है, telescope भारी दूरियों पर बड़ी objects. हर design का चुनाव उसी एक फ़र्क़ से बहता है।
तो focal length के नुस्ख़े उल्टे हैं। Microscope दोनों focal lengths छोटी चाहता है, दोनों चरणों पर ख़ूब magnify करने को। Telescope लंबी objective और छोटी eyepiece चाहता है।
Magnification के formulas भी अलग हैं। Microscope दो चरण गुणा करता है, objective linear गुणा eyepiece angular. Telescope बस दोनों focal lengths का अनुपात लेता है।
अब आँख, हर शृंखला का आख़िरी instrument. उसका अपना lens images को retina पर focus करता है, और वो अपना आकार बदलकर focal length adjust करता है, इस प्रक्रिया को accommodation कहते हैं।
ये जानी पहचानी चीज़ें समझाता है। उम्र के साथ पीछे हटता near point ही reading glasses आम बनाता है। और near sighted या far sighted आँख क्रमशः diverging या converging lens से ठीक होती है।
तो इस subtopic का हर instrument आख़िरकार अपनी image इसी एक कमाल के lens को सौंप देता है। Microscope और telescope बस रोशनी तैयार करते हैं, retina पर आख़िरी focusing आँख करती है।

sections.title: The microscope toolkit

board_events.text: Magnifying powers for the microscopes
Magnifying power is always the angular ratio: angle with the instrument over angle without it. $D = 25$ cm is the near point of a normal eye.
In the compound formula, the eyepiece term is $D/f_e$ for a relaxed eye or $1+D/f_e$ at the near point.
All magnifying powers are pure numbers, dimensionless. Focal lengths and distances are lengths.
For high microscope power, both focal lengths should be short: a short objective and a short eyepiece both raise the magnification.

segments.text: This is the working set for the microscopes. Everything traces back to one definition, and then splits by which instrument and which eye setting you have.
The root definition, first. The magnifying power is always the angular ratio: the angle the image subtends with the instrument, divided by the angle the object subtends without it.
And one fixed number underlies them all. The near point of a normal eye, capital D, is twenty five centimetres, the closest the eye can focus without strain.
The simple microscope with a relaxed eye is the cleanest case. The magnifying power is simply D over the focal length, with the final image at infinity.
Strain the eye to bring the image to the near point instead, and you gain one unit: the magnifying power becomes one plus D over the focal length.
The compound microscope multiplies two stages. The objective contributes its image distance over its object distance, and the eyepiece contributes D over its focal length.
The eyepiece term follows the same relaxed-versus-near-point split as the simple microscope: D over the eyepiece focal length for a relaxed eye, or one plus that at the near point.
The units are easy. Every magnifying power is a ratio of two angles, so it is a pure number, dimensionless. The focal lengths and the distances are ordinary lengths.

And the design lesson, worth stating as a formula reader's rule. For high microscope power, both focal lengths should be short, because a short objective and a short eyepiece each raise the magnification.
ये microscopes का working set है। सब कुछ एक परिभाषा पर लौटता है, फिर इस पर बँटता है कि कौन सा instrument और कौन सी आँख की setting है।
पहले मूल परिभाषा। Magnifying power हमेशा कोणीय अनुपात है, instrument के साथ image जो कोण बनाती है, बटा उसके बिना object जो कोण बनाती है।
और एक तय number इन सबके नीचे है। सामान्य आँख का near point, capital D, पच्चीस centimetre है, वो सबसे पास जहाँ आँख बिना ज़ोर के focus कर सके।
आराम में आँख वाला simple microscope सबसे साफ़ case है। Magnifying power बस D बटा focal length है, final image अनंत पर।
इसके बजाय आँख को ज़ोर देकर image को near point पर लाइए, तो एक इकाई मिलती है, magnifying power बन जाती है one plus D बटा focal length।
Compound microscope दो चरण गुणा करता है। Objective देता है अपना image distance बटा अपना object distance, और eyepiece देता है D बटा अपनी focal length।
Eyepiece वाला term वही relaxed बनाम near point बँटवारा मानता है जो simple microscope में था, आराम में D बटा eyepiece focal length, या near point पर one plus वो।
Units आसान हैं। हर magnifying power दो कोणों का अनुपात है, तो शुद्ध संख्या, dimensionless. Focal lengths और distances साधारण lengths हैं।
और design वाला सबक़, formula पढ़ने वाले के नियम की तरह। ऊँची microscope power के लिए दोनों focal lengths छोटी चाहिए, क्योंकि छोटी objective और छोटी eyepiece दोनों magnification बढ़ाती हैं।

sections.title: The telescope toolkit, and the reflex to carry

board_events.text: Magnifying power and tube length
Note the inversion between the two forms. In focal lengths the objective is on top; in powers the eyepiece is on top.
The near-point form gives slightly more magnification, at the cost of a strained eye. Normal adjustment is the default unless a question says otherwise.

board_events.text: A telescope wants a long objective and a short eyepiece, the reverse of a microscope. Both magnifying powers are dimensionless.
Remember to convert dioptre to metres before use: a power of 25 D means a focal length of 4 cm, not 25 cm.

segments.text: The telescope toolkit is short, but it hides two reflexes worth carrying, because both save real time and both are easy to get backwards.
The core pair, in normal adjustment. The magnifying power is the objective focal length over the eyepiece focal length, and the tube length is the sum of the two.
Now the reflex that saves conversions. When powers are given rather than focal lengths, the magnifying power is simply the eyepiece power over the objective power.

Watch the inversion carefully, because it is where the marks leak. In the focal-length form the objective is on top; in the power form the eyepiece is on top. They are reciprocals, so the order flips.
There is also a near-point form, used when the final image is brought to twenty five centimetres rather than infinity. It gives a little more magnification, through an extra bracketed factor.
That near-point form costs a strained eye, so normal adjustment is the default. Reach for it only when a question explicitly places the image at the near point.
The board contrasts the two instruments once more, because the design goals are the single most confused point. A telescope wants a long objective and a short eyepiece.
That is the exact reverse of the microscope, which wanted both short. And as always, both magnifying powers are dimensionless, being ratios of like quantities.

One last operational warning, the one that spoils otherwise correct answers. Convert dioptre to metres before using it: a power of twenty five dioptre means a focal length of four centimetres, not twenty five.
Telescope का toolkit छोटा है, पर उसमें दो reflexes छिपे हैं जो साथ रखने लायक़ हैं, क्योंकि दोनों असली समय बचाते हैं और दोनों को उल्टा कर देना आसान है।
मुख्य जोड़ी, normal adjustment में। Magnifying power है objective focal length बटा eyepiece focal length, और tube length दोनों का जोड़।
अब वो reflex जो conversions बचाता है। जब focal lengths के बजाय powers दी हों, magnifying power बस eyepiece power बटा objective power है।
उलटाव को ध्यान से देखिए, क्योंकि यहीं marks रिसते हैं। Focal length वाले रूप में objective ऊपर है, power वाले में eyepiece ऊपर। वो व्युत्क्रम हैं, तो क्रम पलट जाता है।
एक near point रूप भी है, जो तब काम आता है जब final image अनंत के बजाय पच्चीस centimetre पर लाई जाए। वो एक अतिरिक्त bracket वाले factor से थोड़ा ज़्यादा magnification देता है।
वो near point रूप आँख के तनाव की क़ीमत माँगता है, इसलिए normal adjustment default है। इसे सिर्फ़ तब उठाइए जब सवाल साफ़ तौर पर image को near point पर रखे।
Board दोनों instruments का अंतर एक बार फिर दिखाता है, क्योंकि design के लक्ष्य सबसे ज़्यादा भ्रमित करने वाली बात हैं। Telescope लंबी objective और छोटी eyepiece चाहता है।
ये microscope का बिल्कुल उल्टा है, जो दोनों छोटी चाहता था। और हमेशा की तरह, दोनों magnifying powers dimensionless हैं, क्योंकि वो एक जैसी राशियों के अनुपात हैं।
एक आख़िरी operational चेतावनी, वही जो सही जवाब बिगाड़ती है। इस्तेमाल से पहले dioptre को metres में बदलिए, पच्चीस dioptre की power का मतलब चार centimetre focal length है, पच्चीस नहीं।

board_events.text: A convex lens of focal length 5 cm is used as a magnifying glass. Find its magnifying power (a) for a relaxed eye and (b) with the image at the near point.
So the same lens gives five times magnification relaxed, or six times with the eye strained to the near point.
The near-point setting always gains exactly one unit over the relaxed setting. That constant difference is a quick check.
Which to quote depends on the wording. Relaxed or normal means $D/f$; maximum or near point means $1+D/f$.

segments.text: Begin at board level, with the simple microscope and its two settings. The whole point is to read the question's wording and pick the right one of two very similar formulas.
The figure shows both magnifications side by side, the relaxed setting and the near-point setting, differing by exactly one unit.
The question. A convex lens of focal length five centimetres is used as a magnifying glass. Find its magnifying power, first for a relaxed eye, and then with the image brought to the near point.
For the relaxed eye the image is at infinity, and the magnifying power is D over f. That is twenty five over five, which is five times.
For the near point, the magnifying power is one plus D over f. That is one plus twenty five over five, which is six times.
So the same lens gives five times magnification with a relaxed eye, or six times when the eye is strained to place the image at the near point.
Notice the pattern, which is a quick check on any such problem. The near-point setting always gains exactly one unit over the relaxed setting, because the two formulas differ only by that plus one.
So which value you quote depends entirely on the wording. Relaxed or normal viewing means D over f. Maximum magnification, or image at the near point, means one plus D over f.
Board level से शुरू, simple microscope और उसकी दो settings के साथ। पूरी बात सवाल के शब्द पढ़कर दो बहुत मिलते जुलते formulas में से सही चुनने की है।
Figure दोनों magnifications आमने सामने दिखाती है, relaxed setting और near point setting, ठीक एक इकाई के फ़र्क़ से।
सवाल ये है। पाँच centimetre focal length वाला convex lens magnifying glass की तरह इस्तेमाल होता है। उसकी magnifying power निकालिए, पहले आराम में आँख के लिए, फिर image को near point पर लाकर।
आराम में आँख के लिए image अनंत पर है, और magnifying power D बटा f है। यानी पच्चीस बटा पाँच, जो पाँच गुना है।
Near point के लिए magnifying power one plus D बटा f है। यानी one plus पच्चीस बटा पाँच, जो छह गुना है।
तो वही lens आराम में आँख के साथ पाँच गुना magnification देता है, या छह गुना जब आँख को ज़ोर देकर image near point पर रखी जाए।
Pattern पर ध्यान दीजिए, जो ऐसे किसी भी सवाल की जल्दी जाँच है। Near point setting हमेशा relaxed setting से ठीक एक इकाई ज़्यादा देती है, क्योंकि दोनों formulas बस उस plus one से अलग हैं।
तो आप कौन सी क़ीमत बताते हैं ये पूरी तरह शब्दों पर है। Relaxed या normal देखना मतलब D बटा f. Maximum magnification, या image near point पर, मतलब one plus D बटा f।

board_events.text: A compound microscope has objective focal length 2 cm, eyepiece focal length 5 cm, and tube length 20 cm. Find the magnifying power at the near point.
The trap: adding the stages to get sixteen. Magnifications in series multiply, they never add.
A quick sanity check: sixty times is a plausible microscope power, while sixteen would be feeble for a two-lens instrument.
Using $L/f_o$ for the objective assumes the object sits close to its focus, the standard textbook approximation.

segments.text: This one is a speed trap built on a single word: the stages multiply, they do not add. Get that right and the arithmetic is trivial.
The figure shows the two stage magnifications separately and then their product, which is the whole answer.

The question. A compound microscope has an objective focal length of two centimetres, an eyepiece focal length of five centimetres, and a tube length of twenty centimetres. Find the magnifying power at the near point.
First the objective. Its magnification is approximately the tube length over its focal length, which is twenty over two, that is ten.
Then the eyepiece, at the near point. Its magnification is one plus D over its focal length, which is one plus twenty five over five, that is six.
The total magnifying power is the product of the two, ten times six, which is sixty times.
Here is the trap. Students add the stages and get sixteen. But magnifications in series always multiply, they never add, because each stage magnifies the image the previous stage produced.
A quick sanity check confirms it. Sixty times is a thoroughly plausible microscope power, whereas sixteen would be feeble for a two-lens instrument, barely better than a single magnifying glass.

One assumption is quietly at work. Using tube length over objective focal length assumes the object sits very close to the objective's focus, which is the standard textbook approximation for a compound microscope.
ये एक speed trap है जो एक ही शब्द पर बना है, चरण गुणा होते हैं, जुड़ते नहीं। वो सही कर लीजिए और arithmetic मामूली है।
Figure दोनों चरण magnifications अलग अलग दिखाती है और फिर उनका गुणनफल, जो पूरा जवाब है।
सवाल ये है। एक compound microscope की objective focal length दो centimetre, eyepiece focal length पाँच centimetre, और tube length बीस centimetre है। Near point पर magnifying power निकालिए।
पहले objective. उसका magnification लगभग tube length बटा उसकी focal length है, यानी बीस बटा दो, जो दस है।
फिर eyepiece, near point पर। उसका magnification one plus D बटा उसकी focal length है, यानी one plus पच्चीस बटा पाँच, जो छह है।
कुल magnifying power दोनों का गुणनफल है, दस गुना छह, जो साठ गुना है।
यही जाल है। Students चरण जोड़ देते हैं और सोलह पाते हैं। पर शृंखला में magnifications हमेशा गुणा होते हैं, कभी जुड़ते नहीं, क्योंकि हर चरण पिछले चरण की बनाई image को बड़ा करता है।
एक जल्दी sanity check इसकी पुष्टि करता है। साठ गुना एक भरोसेमंद microscope power है, जबकि सोलह दो lens वाले instrument के लिए कमज़ोर होता, अकेले magnifying glass से बमुश्किल बेहतर।

एक assumption चुपचाप काम कर रहा है। Tube length बटा objective focal length इस्तेमाल करना ये मानता है कि object objective के focus के बहुत पास बैठी है, जो compound microscope की standard textbook approximation है।

board_events.text: A telescope has an objective of power 0.5 D and an eyepiece of power 25 D. Find the magnifying power in normal adjustment and the tube length.
The direct route, $M = P_e/P_o$, skips both focal-length conversions. Note the eyepiece power is on top.
The classic slip here is treating 25 D as 25 cm. Always convert: a power of 25 D is a focal length of 4 cm.

segments.text: A main-level telescope problem, and the real lesson is that when powers are given, there is a shortcut that skips the focal-length conversions entirely.
The figure lays out both routes: the long way through focal lengths, and the direct power ratio that gets there in one step.
The question. A telescope has an objective of power nought point five dioptre and an eyepiece of power twenty five dioptre. Find the magnifying power in normal adjustment and the tube length.

The long route first. Convert each power to a focal length. The objective is one over nought point five, that is two metres, or two hundred centimetres. The eyepiece is one over twenty five, that is four centimetres.
Then the magnifying power is the objective focal length over the eyepiece, two hundred over four, which is fifty times.
The short route gets there directly. The magnifying power is the eyepiece power over the objective power, twenty five over nought point five, which is fifty times, with no conversions at all.
The tube length still needs the focal lengths, though. It is their sum, two hundred plus four, which is two hundred and four centimetres.
Carry the shortcut as a reflex. The magnifying power is the eyepiece power over the objective power, and note carefully that the eyepiece is on top, the inverse of the focal-length form.

The classic slip here is treating twenty five dioptre as twenty five centimetres. Always convert first: a power of twenty five dioptre is a focal length of four centimetres, and mistaking the two wrecks the answer.
एक main level telescope सवाल, और असली सबक़ ये है कि जब powers दी हों, तो एक shortcut है जो focal length conversions पूरी तरह छोड़ देता है।
Figure दोनों रास्ते सामने रखती है, focal lengths वाला लंबा रास्ता, और सीधा power ratio जो एक ही step में पहुँचा देता है।
सवाल ये है। एक telescope की objective की power शून्य point पाँच dioptre और eyepiece की पच्चीस dioptre है। Normal adjustment में magnifying power और tube length निकालिए।
पहले लंबा रास्ता। हर power को focal length में बदलिए। Objective है एक बटा शून्य point पाँच, यानी दो metre, या दो सौ centimetre. Eyepiece है एक बटा पच्चीस, यानी चार centimetre।
फिर magnifying power है objective focal length बटा eyepiece, दो सौ बटा चार, जो पचास गुना है।
छोटा रास्ता सीधे पहुँचता है। Magnifying power है eyepiece power बटा objective power, पच्चीस बटा शून्य point पाँच, जो पचास गुना है, बिना किसी conversion के।
Tube length को फिर भी focal lengths चाहिए। वो उनका जोड़ है, दो सौ plus चार, यानी दो सौ चार centimetre।
Shortcut को reflex की तरह रखिए। Magnifying power है eyepiece power बटा objective power, और ध्यान से देखिए कि eyepiece ऊपर है, focal length वाले रूप का उल्टा।
यहाँ classic चूक पच्चीस dioptre को पच्चीस centimetre मान लेना है। हमेशा पहले बदलिए, पच्चीस dioptre की power चार centimetre focal length है, और दोनों को मिला देना जवाब बिगाड़ देता है।

<svg viewBox="0 0 956 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
<text x="20" y="26" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Telescope from M = 24 and tube length 100 cm</text>
<rect x="20" y="48" width="350" height="45" rx="8" fill="#e6ebee"/>
<text x="36" y="76" font-size="12.5" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Two equations in normal adjustment:</text>
<text x="36" y="104" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">M = f₊ / f₋ = 24</text>
<text x="36" y="128" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">L = f₊ + f₋ = 100 cm</text>
<text x="36" y="160" font-size="12.5" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">From the first, f₊ = 24 f₋. Substitute:</text>
<text x="36" y="188" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">24 f₋ + f₋ = 25 f₋ = 100</text>
<text x="36" y="220" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#b3402f" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">f₋ = 4 cm, f₊ = 96 cm</text>
<text x="36" y="256" font-size="11.5" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Check: 96 / 4 = 24 and 96 + 4 = 100. Both hold.</text>
<rect x="420" y="48" width="350" height="45" rx="8" fill="#22303c"/>
<text x="436" y="76" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">The standard two-equation setup</text>
<text x="436" y="106" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Whenever a telescope problem gives you</text>
<text x="436" y="126" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">the magnification and the tube length,</text>
<text x="436" y="146" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">write M = f₊/f₋ and L = f₊+f₋ and solve.</text>
<text x="436" y="182" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">The neat trick: f₊ = M f₋, so</text>
<text x="436" y="202" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">L = (M + 1) f₋, giving f₋ = L / (M+1)</text>
<text x="436" y="222" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">in a single line.</text>
<text x="436" y="256" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Here f₋ = 100 / 25 = 4 cm at once.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: A telescope in normal adjustment has a magnifying power of 24 and a tube length of 100 cm. Find the two focal lengths.
Two relations hold at once: the magnifying power is the ratio of focal lengths, and the tube length is their sum.
The neat trick: $f_o = M f_e$ turns the tube length into $(M+1)f_e = L$, so $f_e = L/(M+1) = 100/25 = 4$ cm in one line.
Check: $96/4 = 24$ and $96 + 4 = 100$. Both conditions hold, so the answer is safe.

segments.text: Advanced level to finish, and it is a clean two-equation problem: given the magnifying power and the tube length, recover the two focal lengths.
The figure shows the pair of equations and how they combine. Two unknowns, two conditions, and a tidy substitution that solves them in a line.
The question. A telescope in normal adjustment has a magnifying power of twenty four and a tube length of one hundred centimetres. Find the objective and eyepiece focal lengths.
Two relations hold at the same time. The magnifying power is the objective focal length over the eyepiece focal length, and the tube length is the sum of the two.
Write them out. The first says the objective over the eyepiece is twenty four. The second says the two focal lengths add to one hundred centimetres.
From the first, the objective is twenty four times the eyepiece. Substitute that into the second: twenty four eyepiece plus one eyepiece is twenty five eyepiece, equal to one hundred.
So the eyepiece focal length is one hundred over twenty five, that is four centimetres, and the objective is the remaining ninety six centimetres.

There is a neat trick worth carrying. Since the objective is the magnification times the eyepiece, the tube length becomes the magnification plus one, times the eyepiece. So the eyepiece is the tube length over the magnification plus one, four centimetres in a single step.
Finish with the check. Ninety six over four is twenty four, and ninety six plus four is one hundred. Both conditions hold, so the answer is safe.
ख़त्म करने के लिए advanced level, और ये एक साफ़ दो समीकरण वाला सवाल है, magnifying power और tube length दिए हों तो दोनों focal lengths निकालिए।
Figure समीकरणों की जोड़ी और उनके मिलने का तरीक़ा दिखाती है। दो अनजान, दो conditions, और एक साफ़ substitution जो उन्हें एक line में हल कर देता है।
सवाल ये है। Normal adjustment में एक telescope की magnifying power चौबीस और tube length एक सौ centimetre है। Objective और eyepiece focal lengths निकालिए।
दो relations एक साथ चलते हैं। Magnifying power है objective focal length बटा eyepiece focal length, और tube length दोनों का जोड़।
उन्हें लिखिए। पहला कहता है objective बटा eyepiece बराबर चौबीस। दूसरा कहता है दोनों focal lengths जुड़कर एक सौ centimetre।
पहले से, objective चौबीस गुना eyepiece है। इसे दूसरे में डालिए, चौबीस eyepiece plus एक eyepiece बराबर पच्चीस eyepiece, जो एक सौ के बराबर।
तो eyepiece focal length है एक सौ बटा पच्चीस, यानी चार centimetre, और objective बची हुई छियानवे centimetre।

एक साफ़ चाल साथ रखने लायक़ है। Objective, magnification गुणा eyepiece है, तो tube length बन जाता है magnification plus one गुणा eyepiece. यानी eyepiece है tube length बटा magnification plus one, एक ही step में चार centimetre।
जाँच से ख़त्म कीजिए। छियानवे बटा चार बराबर चौबीस, और छियानवे plus चार बराबर एक सौ। दोनों conditions सही हैं, तो जवाब पक्का है।

board_events.caption: The four traps, and the memory aids that block them

<svg viewBox="0 0 914 338" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif">
<text x="20" y="26" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Where optical-instrument questions go wrong</text>
<rect x="20" y="42" width="350" height="45" rx="6" fill="#e6ebee"/>
<text x="36" y="63" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#b3402f" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">1. Mixing the two magnifying-power formulas</text>
<text x="36" y="83" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Relaxed eye: M = D/f. Near point: M = 1 + D/f. Read whether the image is at infinity or at 25 cm.</text>
<rect x="20" y="100" width="350" height="45" rx="6" fill="#f4f7f8"/>
<text x="36" y="121" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#b3402f" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">2. Adding magnifications instead of multiplying</text>
<text x="36" y="141" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">In a compound microscope, M = m₊ × m₋. The stages chain, they do not sum.</text>
<rect x="20" y="158" width="350" height="45" rx="6" fill="#e6ebee"/>
<text x="36" y="179" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#b3402f" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">3. Inverting the telescope ratio</text>
<text x="36" y="199" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">M = f₊/f₋ but M = P₋/P₊. Focal length has objective on top; power has eyepiece on top.</text>
<rect x="20" y="216" width="350" height="45" rx="6" fill="#f4f7f8"/>
<text x="36" y="237" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#b3402f" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">4. Forgetting to convert dioptre to metres</text>
<text x="36" y="257" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">P = 1/f needs f in metres. A power of 25 D is f = 4 cm, not 25 cm.</text>
<rect x="20" y="274" width="350" height="45" rx="6" fill="#22303c"/>
<text x="36" y="296" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Memory aids: microscope wants both focal lengths short; telescope wants the objective long, eyepiece short.</text>
<text x="36" y="318" font-size="12.5" fill="#ffffff" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Near point adds one. Magnifications multiply. And for a telescope M = P eyepiece over P objective.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Mixing the two magnifying-power formulas. Relaxed eye gives $M = D/f$; near point gives $M = 1 + D/f$. Read whether the image is at infinity or at 25 cm.
Adding magnifications instead of multiplying. In a compound microscope $M = m_o \times M_e$. The stages chain, they never sum.
Inverting the telescope ratio. In focal lengths $M = f_o/f_e$, but in powers $M = P_e/P_o$. Objective on top for focal length, eyepiece on top for power.
Forgetting to convert dioptre to metres. $P = 1/f$ needs $f$ in metres, so 25 D is a focal length of 4 cm, not 25 cm.
Reflex one: a microscope wants both focal lengths short; a telescope wants a long objective and a short eyepiece.
Reflex two: the near-point setting always adds one unit; magnifications multiply; and for a telescope $M = P_e/P_o$.
Memory aids: angle not size, near point adds one, stages multiply, and dioptre needs metres.

segments.text: To close the chapter's last subtopic, here is where instrument marks actually leak. All four are formula-selection or units errors, not conceptual gaps.
The board lists them in the order they cost marks, with the memory aids underneath. This is the final page to reread before the paper.
First, mixing the two magnifying-power formulas. A relaxed eye gives D over f, the near point one plus D over f. Read whether the image is at infinity or at twenty five centimetres.
Second, adding magnifications instead of multiplying. In a compound microscope the total is the objective magnification times the eyepiece magnification. The stages chain in series, they never sum.
Third, inverting the telescope ratio. In focal lengths it is the objective over the eyepiece; in powers, the eyepiece over the objective. Objective on top for focal length, eyepiece on top for power.
Fourth, forgetting to convert dioptre to metres. Power is one over the focal length in metres, so twenty five dioptre is a focal length of four centimetres, never twenty five.

Now the reflexes. A microscope wants both focal lengths short, to magnify strongly at both stages. A telescope wants a long objective and a short eyepiece. That single contrast settles most design questions.

The second reflex bundles three quick facts. The near-point setting always adds one unit over relaxed. Magnifications in series multiply. And for a telescope the magnifying power is the eyepiece power over the objective power.
Finally the memory aids, four short phrases. Angle not size. Near point adds one. Stages multiply. And dioptre needs metres. Those four carry almost every instrument question safely.
Chapter के आख़िरी subtopic को बंद करने के लिए, यहाँ instrument के marks असल में रिसते हैं। चारों formula चुनने या units की ग़लतियाँ हैं, concept की कमी नहीं।
Board उन्हें उसी क्रम में गिनाता है जिसमें वो marks खाते हैं, नीचे memory aids हैं। Paper से पहले यही आख़िरी page दोबारा पढ़िए।
पहली, दोनों magnifying power formulas मिला देना। आराम में आँख देती है D बटा f, near point one plus D बटा f. पढ़िए image अनंत पर है या पच्चीस centimetre पर।
दूसरी, magnifications गुणा करने के बजाय जोड़ देना। Compound microscope में कुल है objective magnification गुणा eyepiece magnification. चरण शृंखला में जुड़ते हैं, कभी जमा नहीं होते।
तीसरी, telescope का अनुपात उलट देना। Focal lengths में objective बटा eyepiece, powers में eyepiece बटा objective. Focal length के लिए objective ऊपर, power के लिए eyepiece ऊपर।
चौथी, dioptre को metres में बदलना भूलना। Power है एक बटा focal length metres में, तो पच्चीस dioptre चार centimetre focal length है, कभी पच्चीस नहीं।
अब reflexes. Microscope दोनों focal lengths छोटी चाहता है, दोनों चरणों पर ख़ूब magnify करने को। Telescope लंबी objective और छोटी eyepiece चाहता है। वही एक अंतर ज़्यादातर design सवाल तय कर देता है।

दूसरा reflex तीन जल्दी तथ्य बाँधता है। Near point setting हमेशा relaxed से एक इकाई जोड़ती है। शृंखला में magnifications गुणा होते हैं। और telescope के लिए magnifying power eyepiece power बटा objective power है।
आख़िर में memory aids, चार छोटे वाक्य। कोण, आकार नहीं। Near point एक जोड़ता है। चरण गुणा होते हैं। और dioptre को metres चाहिए। वो चार लगभग हर instrument सवाल सुरक्षित निकाल देते हैं।

board_events.text: This is a recap, not a re-teaching. Every relation here was derived and used earlier; the board simply gathers them so you can see the whole chapter at a glance.

segments.text: Before the final cheat sheet, one consolidating board that gathers every formula in the chapter into a single view. Nothing here is new; it is all restated for revision.
The diagram is the complete formula sheet, grouped by topic. Keep it as the one page to photograph before an examination, because everything the chapter can ask sits on it.
Start with mirrors, from the first part. The mirror formula adds the object and image terms, the focal length is half the radius, and the magnification is minus v over u.

Then refraction and total internal reflection. Snell's law relates the two indices and angles, the critical angle has its sine equal to one over the index, and apparent depth is the real depth divided by the index.
Next the curved-surface pair. The single-surface relation carries the index jump over the radius, and the lens-maker's formula builds the focal length from the material and the two radii.
Then the thin lens itself. Its formula subtracts the object term, the magnification is plus v over u, the power is one over the focal length, and powers simply add for lenses in contact.

Now the prism group. The deviation is incidence plus emergence minus apex, the internal angles sum to the apex, the prism formula gives the index at minimum deviation, and the dispersive power is the standard ratio.

Finally the instruments. The simple microscope is D over f, or one plus that at the near point; the telescope power is the objective over the eyepiece focal length, or the eyepiece over the objective power.
Read this as a recap, not a re-teaching. Every relation here was derived and used earlier. Gathering them in one place lets you see the whole structure of ray optics at a glance.
आख़िरी cheat sheet से पहले, एक consolidating board जो chapter का हर formula एक ही नज़र में इकट्ठा कर देता है। यहाँ कुछ नया नहीं, सब revision के लिए दोबारा रखा गया है।
Diagram पूरी formula sheet है, topic के हिसाब से बँटी। इसे परीक्षा से पहले photo खींचने वाला एक page मानिए, क्योंकि chapter जो कुछ पूछ सकता है वो सब इसी पर है।
पहले हिस्से वाले mirrors से शुरू कीजिए। Mirror formula object और image terms जोड़ता है, focal length radius की आधी है, और magnification minus v बटा u है।
फिर refraction और total internal reflection. Snell's law दोनों indices और कोणों को जोड़ता है, critical angle का sine एक बटा index है, और apparent depth असली गहराई बटा index है।
अगली है curved surface वाली जोड़ी। Single surface relation index का अंतर बटा radius लेकर चलता है, और lens maker formula focal length को material और दोनों radii से बनाता है।
फिर thin lens ख़ुद। उसका formula object term घटाता है, magnification plus v बटा u है, power एक बटा focal length है, और संपर्क में रखे lenses के लिए powers बस जुड़ जाती हैं।
अब prism समूह। Deviation है incidence plus emergence minus apex, internal angles apex में जुड़ते हैं, prism formula minimum deviation पर index देता है, और dispersive power standard अनुपात है।
आख़िर में instruments. Simple microscope है D बटा f, या near point पर one plus वो, और telescope की power है objective बटा eyepiece focal length, या eyepiece बटा objective power।
इसे recap समझिए, दोबारा पढ़ाना नहीं। इसका हर relation पहले निकाला और इस्तेमाल हो चुका है। उन्हें एक जगह इकट्ठा करना ray optics की पूरी संरचना एक नज़र में दिखा देता है।

board_events.text: Sign discipline first. A real object always has $u$ negative. The mirror formula adds the object term, the lens formula subtracts it, and their magnifications carry opposite signs.
Instant reflexes: a concave lens and a convex mirror always give a virtual, erect, diminished image. A small critical angle means a large index.
The prism formula holds only at minimum deviation. Violet bends most, red least. Powers add in contact; magnifications multiply in series.

The four traps that cost the most: measuring angles from the surface not the normal; importing the mirror's plus sign into a lens; giving both radii the same sign; and forgetting that a dioptre needs $f$ in metres.
The exam-hall drill: signs first, algebra second. State the image's nature before you compute, then let the numbers confirm it.
A sanity check that contradicts your sign is the sign warning you, not the physics failing. Trust the qualitative reasoning and re-examine the arithmetic.
That single habit, predicting the answer's character before calculating, catches nearly every sign error this chapter can produce.

segments.text: And now the final board of the chapter: the single cheat sheet to carry into the examination. It is not new physics but the distilled discipline that keeps the physics from going wrong.
The diagram holds three panels: the sign conventions, the instant reflexes that eliminate wrong options, and the handful of traps that cost the most marks. This is the last thing to review.

Sign discipline comes first, because it causes the most lost marks. A real object always has a negative object distance. The mirror formula adds the object term, the lens subtracts it, and their magnifications carry opposite signs.

Now the instant reflexes, which eliminate options before any algebra. A concave lens and a convex mirror both always give a virtual, erect, diminished image. And a small critical angle means a large refractive index.

Three more reflexes for the later topics. The prism formula holds only at minimum deviation, never elsewhere. Violet bends most and red least. And powers add for lenses in contact, while magnifications multiply for stages in series.

Then the four costliest traps. Measuring angles from the surface not the normal. Importing the mirror's plus sign into a lens or refraction relation. Giving both radii the same sign. And forgetting a dioptre needs the focal length in metres.

Above all, carry the exam-hall drill. Signs first, algebra second. State the nature of the image, real or virtual, erect or inverted, before you compute anything, and then let the numbers confirm what you already predicted.

And trust that prediction. If a sanity check contradicts your sign, that is the sign warning you of an error, not the physics failing. Trust the qualitative reasoning and go back to re-examine the arithmetic.

That single habit, predicting the character of the answer before calculating it, catches nearly every sign error this chapter can produce. Master it, and ray optics becomes one of the most reliable scoring chapters in the paper.
और अब chapter का आख़िरी board, वो अकेली cheat sheet जो परीक्षा में साथ ले जानी है। ये नई physics नहीं है बल्कि वो निचोड़ा हुआ अनुशासन है जो physics को ग़लत होने से बचाता है।
Diagram में तीन panels हैं, sign conventions, वो instant reflexes जो ग़लत options हटा देते हैं, और वो चंद traps जो सबसे ज़्यादा marks खाते हैं। यही आख़िरी चीज़ है दोहराने की।

पहले sign discipline, क्योंकि यही सबसे ज़्यादा marks खाता है। Real object का object distance हमेशा negative होता है। Mirror formula object term जोड़ता है, lens घटाता है, और उनके magnifications उल्टे signs लेते हैं।

अब instant reflexes, जो algebra से पहले options हटाते हैं। Concave lens और convex mirror दोनों हमेशा virtual, erect, diminished image देते हैं। और छोटा critical angle बड़ा refractive index मतलब रखता है।

बाद के topics के लिए तीन और reflexes. Prism formula सिर्फ़ minimum deviation पर चलता है, और कहीं नहीं। Violet सबसे ज़्यादा और red सबसे कम मुड़ता है। और संपर्क में powers जुड़ती हैं, जबकि शृंखला में magnifications गुणा होते हैं।

फिर चार सबसे महँगे traps. Normal के बजाय surface से कोण नापना। Mirror का plus sign lens या refraction relation में उठा लाना। दोनों radii को एक ही sign देना। और dioptre को focal length metres में चाहिए ये भूलना।

सबसे बढ़कर, exam hall वाली drill साथ रखिए। पहले signs, फिर algebra. Image का स्वभाव बताइए, real या virtual, erect या inverted, कुछ भी compute करने से पहले, और फिर numbers से पुष्टि होने दीजिए जो आपने पहले ही बता दिया।

और उस भविष्यवाणी पर भरोसा कीजिए। अगर sanity check आपके sign का खंडन करे, तो वो sign आपको ग़लती की चेतावनी दे रहा है, physics नाकाम नहीं हो रही। Qualitative तर्क पर भरोसा कीजिए और arithmetic दोबारा जाँचिए।
वही एक आदत, जवाब का स्वभाव गिनने से पहले बता देना, इस chapter की लगभग हर sign ग़लती पकड़ लेती है। इसमें महारत पाइए, और ray optics paper के सबसे भरोसेमंद scoring chapters में से एक बन जाता है।
